I wish to revert to the question of information respecting these tariff resolutions. The Minister of Finance brought down a little pamphlet showing the alterations that would be made if this agreement went through, but outside of that there is practically no information that we can get unless we go to the several blue-books that are brought before this House annually. What is the result? The result is that members on both sides of the House derive their information from blue-books, and contradictory statements are consequently made, so that the public are not sure who is right. Why should we not have supplied by the government full and definite information such as the House at Washington had when these matters were placed before them? The refusal of the Minister of Finance to furnish such a statement convinces me that the minister does not want to give the public the information necessary for them to judge whether or not this is a correct bargain. Why should the minister try to blindfold the people, or not to give information? In making his announcement, the minister did not inform us as to the other favoured nation countries that -would enjoy the benefit of this agreement, but when the member for South Ontario asked what other countries would be affected the answer was such that the pe'ople could read it either one way or another, and a newspaper in eastern Canada quoted that statement to show that statements made in this House that other countries would have the benefit of this arrangement were not true. We must see the effect of every change in each item on the different parts of the country. The Minister of Finance deliberately, and, I might- say, if it were within parliamentary rules, wilfully tried to keep information back to prevent us properly enlightening the people of this country. I, as a member of this House, demand as a right that we should receive this information. I think we are entitled to it. and if the minister
wants to get these resolutions through in any kind of reasonable time, if he'will give this information he will get them through a great deal quicker than by holding back this information. We should have the amount of imports and exports of each of these items, and we should also have the exports from other countries, with the rates of duties, prices, &c. If the minister thinks that he can drive these resolutions through by blindfolding the people he is making an awful mistake. I am going to get this information; if we cannot get it one way we will have to keep at it until we do. The minister must give us the information in his possession, and if he will not give it in pamphlet form, so that we can read it intelligently, he will have to give it in the House. That is what he is paid for by the people of the country, and he has to do it. I will do my duty in seeing that he does do it.

When the committee adjourned last night I was making the argument that an arrangement, to be of lasting benefit and permanent, must be a bargain that will give advantages to both sides. Let me give one or two instances to show how the benefits, undeir the proposed agreement, will accrue both to the United States and Canada. Some time ago I read an address to the right hon. the Prime Minister in pamphlet form against this proposed arrangement, and in that address I noticed particularly some words spoken by Mr. Wm. White, vice-president of the Canadian Pacific railway. Mr. White said:
That the Canadian Pacific railway has had to purchase in Winnipeg for their dining cars chickens from Chicago, and were also importing cream from the United States.
I suppose it is fair to presume that if the Canadian Pacific railway had to buy poultry and cream for use in Winnipeg from the United States, other residents of Winnipeg had to do likewise. This we can readily understand because we know that the farmers around Winnipeg are not engaged in raising dairy products, but rather in growing grain and feeding stock. Had there been no duty, the Winnipeg people would have been able to get their cream and poultry from the United States at so much less. But, Sir, at the very time when the people in Winnipeg were finding it to their advantage to buy poultry and cream in the United States, the farmers of Ontario and Quebec were selling their cream in large quantities to the people of the United States just across the border. The people of the province of Quebec sold in the United States last year, even with a small duty in the way, cream to the value of nearly $1,000,000; and the dairymen of Ontario shipped cream to the United States last year to the value of between $500,000 and $1,000,000. Then, the removal of the duty on this item of cream would be to the advantage of the United States farmers who sell cream and also to the advantage of the Canadian farmers who sell cream as well as to the Canadian and American consumers of this article. Let me mention another similar ease . I have here a brief account, which appeared in the Montreal *' Gazette ' February 4 last, of a meeting of the Boston Fruit and Produce Exchange, held the day before. It says:
The members of the Boston Fruit and Produce Exchange voted to petition the Massachusetts senators and representatives in Congress to support to-day the Canadian reciprocity agreement. A resolution was adopted declaring that the members heartily commend the terms of the agreement. The resolution points out that thousands of barrels of apples are yearly shipped from Canada to Europe, and expresses the belief that if free trade is established Canadian producers will ship their apples to the middle west, leaving a large portion of the foreign trade to New England farmers.
This is a declaration by the practical fruit growers of the eastern states, that, if this agreement were in force, they would find a better market for their apples, without the competition of Canadian fruit growers, in the markets, of Europe, and that the Canadian apple grower would find a market fop his fruit in the middle states, thus benefiting the producers of apples in both places, and not raising the price to consumers in either country, but probably having the contrary effect of reducing the prices. The hon. member for North Toronto argued, and several other hon. members have made the same argument, that the reciprocity secured under this agreement will be largely a sectional, occasional reciprocity. The hon. member (Mr. Foster) instanced hay, as an illustration. He said when, in case of drought or for other cause, hay was a short crop in the United States, the Canadian crop of hay would find a market across the line. But he said that if, under such circumstances, the United States required our hay, they would buy it and pay the duty. But he pointed out-and to some extent he was right-that, under this agreement, we not only obtained a market in the United States, but that we give a market in Canada to the people of the United States. This arrangement, in exceptional years and under exceptional circumstances, will have the tendency to regulate prices and to prevent the prices being exorbitant in any part of either country. For instance, I remember, and other members of the House I am sure will not have forgotten, that in 1895 and 1896, in the western part of Ontario, and also extending into the Kingston district and other parts of eastern Ontario, long-continued dry weather caused hay and straw to be very short crops. If, in these two years, we had had no duty upon any hay coming into Ontario from the United States, it would have been a very great benefit to the men who owned cattle on this side of the line at a time when many cattle perished in Canada because of lack of food. The hon. member for North Toronto argued, and others have followed him in this argument also, that the advantage we shall obtain will be a fitful and constantly-changing advantage. Let me read what the hon. gentleman said as to this:

Reciprocity, I think, has this as a prime condition-that it shall be between two countries, each producing a surplus, but a surplus in a different line of articles, and each wanting articles of which the other's surplus is made up. More than that, for ideal reciprocity, this should not be a mere occasional surplus, but should be the result of fixed conditions of climate, soil, and so on, that will make the surplus permanent. Two countries that show ideal conditions of reciprocity in trade would be the West India islands and Canada. The West Indies produce a surplus of tropical fruits, of which we produce none. But they produce absolutely no dairy products, none of the food products of the temperate zone, of which ire produce a great surplus. These are examples of two countries between which a reciprocity trade arrangement could be made with great profit. In the same way, reciprocity between us and Great Britain is possible in lines or articles which will readily suggest themselves to the minds of lion, members. But in the case of the arrangement we are now discussing, you are trying to establish reciprocity between two countries, each of which has a surplus, and a surplus of exactly the same products. With the exception of cheese and fish, the United States of America has a surplus of every article which goes from Canada, under this arrangement, into the United States. And not a slim surplus, but in every .respect a substantial surplus, and in some respects a very large surplus.
The argument, then, is that in Canada our farmers export to Britain products of
the farm; the farmers of the United States export the same thing to the same market and, as they are growers of like produce, and exporters to the same market, this arrangement cannot be of any permanent and steady advantage to Canada. Sir, that is not the case. I will aJdmit, as everybody must admit, that at the present time, the United States is exporting large quantities of certain lines of faTm produce. But I argue-and I can substantiate my argument-that the surplus of the United States is very rapidly decreasing, and it will not be very long until that country has no surplus of farm produce to export. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) helped me in substantiating this argument.	He quoted from the
speech of Congressman McCall, who introduced this resolution in the United States Congress, as saying:
The Canadian surplus of wheat is steadily increasing; ours is steadily diminishing.
That is the fact as to wheat, and it is equally true as to almost every other farm product that the United States is to-day exporting. Let me quote some figures in proof of what I say. I will not go further back than the year 1906, but I give the figures from and including that year, showing the United States exports of farm produce in certain lines:

My hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule), and, I think, also my hon. friend) from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) argued that, while the United States was not exporting as much in live cattle to-day as it did a few years ago, it was exporting chilled and frozen meat in larger quantities than formerly. But the figures prove exactly the contrary. But, Mr. Chairman, if we desired any further evidence as to the falling off in the exports of farm products from the United States, let me refer you to the British Journal of the Board of Agriculture. Speaking of the matter of bacon, this report says that there was a great falling off in the export of bacon from the Mr. MILLER.
United States to Britain in the year 1910. There was exported in that year only 1,307,000 hundred weight, as compared with 2,858.000 hundred weight in 1908. Speaking of the matter of cattle, the above report says:
The past year has seen a further decline in the number of live cattle imported into the United Kingdom, the number received being less than in any year since 1877. Only two countries (apart from the Channel islands) participate in this trade, namely, the United States and Canada, and the diminution in the export is no doubt attributable to the increased demand for cattle in the United States.	i

Then as to the matter of cheese just referred to by the hon. member for Leeds, this journal speaking of the imports of this item, says:	,
The supply of cheese showed a small increase, Canada maintaining its position as the principal exporter. An increase is noticeable in the receipts from New Zealand, while those from the United States have now become of little importance.
Speaking again of flour, this British journal says:
The receipts of flour were less than in 1909, owing to a further falling off from the United States.
Then speaking of the British imports of oats, the journal says:	-
Germany furnishes 2,822,000 hundredweight, while the imports from the United States were insignificant.
iSo we see from this British authority that the imports of Britain of farm products from the United States is very rapidly decreasing. Let me quote from another authority, I quote this from an address delivered by Professor Cyril Hopkins of the University of Illinois. This address was delivered by Professor Hopkins on the 15th of June last, to an association of bankers in the state of Illinois. Professor Hopkins, speaking of the very matter to which I am referring, the rapidly decreasing export and the rapidly decreasing production of food stuffs in the United States, says this:
If we take two five year averages in relation to our exportation of corn and wheat, the two greatest sources of food stuffs in the United States, taking the average for the last five years in the old country, and compare that with the average of the last five years up to the present time, we have figures that are pretty reliable, and exportation products are weighed, and not guessed at, as you know. The products that go out of the country are determined with a high degree of accuracy. The report on crop statistics within the United States is an estimate, but the exportation is not an estimate, it is weighed product. We find by comparing those two five years averages that the exportation of wheat from this country decreased from 37 per cent to 17 per cent of our total production, over a ten year period. We find that the exportation of corn decreased from 9 per cent to 3 per cent of our total production during the same period. Now, those two sets of statistics ought to mean a good deal to us. Our population has been doubling every thirty years for the last century, and the increase is being maintained at nearly the same rate, so far as we can learn yet. And our exportation has decreased until at the present time we export almost no food stuffs compared'with what we produce in America.

speechtext:
Brown, president of the New York Central lines, in an address delivered to the Railway Business Association on the 10th of last November, said:
If our decrease in exportation continues, and if our increased consumption continues, 156
as. compared with our production, before the middle of the next decade the great exporting grain elevators in the sea-board cities will stand empty, and this country, like those of the old world, will be looking for a place to buy the necessities of life.
Now, Sir, these figures mean something to us, as they mean something to the people of the United States. They mean to us that Canada will have an increasing market for her farm products in the United States as the years go by. These figures mean not only that we will have an increased demand for our farm products in the United States, but they mean that the arrangement we are now entering into will be a permanent arrangement. For, Sir, as the years go by, and the United States are less able to produce within their territory the food with which to feed their own people, they will not be so unwise as to cancel an arrangement that enables them to buy food for their people that they will be unable to produce themselves.
Sir, if we will refer to the very able speech made in this House a few evenings ago by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), we will find that we are just beginning to cultivate the soil of Canada. We will find that there is only a small fractional part of the fertile lands' of our northwestern country that has yet been disturbed by the plough. In the years shortly to come we will be producing in Canada a hundred times more farm products than we are producing to-day. But that is not the condition in the United States. Professor Van Heis, of the University of Wisconsin, has recently written a book upon the conservation of the natural resources of the United States; and Professor Van Heis writes as follows:
It is not so many years since we heard the song ' Uncle Sam is rich enough to give us all a farm.' The better part of the public domain has now passed to private parties, and during the closing years of the nineteenth century the land hunger of hundreds of thousands of the citizens of the United States was for the first time unsatisfied.
The hon. member for North Toronto in discussing the matter of natural resources felt justified-and I will not say that he was wrong-in considering the people that are to live in this country a thousand years hence. If any hon. member of this House, in considering the question of the preservation of our resources, is wise in considering the people who shall live in this country a'thousand years hence, then surely we are not less wise in considering what shall be our condition ten or fifteen years hence. It is a matter of importance to secure a trade with the United States that will be of great benefit to us at once and of immensely greater benefit to us in ten or fifteen years hence.

speechtext: Has my hon. friend the figures of the United States production of wheat in 1908, 1909 and 1910 before him?

speechtext: No, I have not, but I have given to my hon. friend and the members of the committee the figures of the exports. I have given them the statement that their surplus is decreasing very rapidly year after year.

speechtext: The production of wheat in the United States in 1909 was 713,000,000 bushels and in 1908, 648,000,000 bushels, an increase in one year of 65,000,000 bushels.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
Yes, but if my hon. friend will take a number of years he will find that the production of wheat in the United States has not been increasing although an increase may be shown by taking an exceptional year. I have pointed out that in one or two other instances the hon. member for North Toronto contradicted his own argument. Let me give the members of the committee a further contradiction, and a very distinct contradiction by that hon. gentleman. He has argued that as Canada is exporting farm products and as the United States is exporting farm products the people of the United States will not require the products of Canadian farms. Then the hon. member for North Toronto in the same speech quotes the following language from President Taft. He says:
And President Taft, in his message to the United States Congress, says that what the United States must set .itself to do is to increase its exports on the line of manufactured goods. That is its future. It eannet expeot to make large exportations of food and other products. What we want, he says, is ran material close at hand; what we want is cheap foodstuffs so far as we can get them from the northern country in order that we may he better provided and furnished for this .increased product and increased export of the industries of this country, in which cur future lies in our record of the world trade.
If any hon. member of this House, whether upon my own side or the other assures me that the United States will not want to buy our farm products, but on the other hand, quotes to me the words of President Taft who says that the people of the United States will want to buy our farm products, I prefer to take the statement, and the opinion of the President of the United States. But, then, Mr. Chairman, there is the mournful argument of Canada becoming the backyard of the United States. I quote from the Toronto ' News ' the following clipping from a speech of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sift on). The Toronto ' News ' gives prominence to this statement of the hon. member. It is printed in large black type and the item is headed ' Backyard of Chicago: '

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
I cannot tell you how 1 feel about this country being made the backyard of the city of Chicago-Hon. Clifford Sifton.
Sir, I happen to own a little backyard behind my own residence, and if somebody will find in that back yard a gold mine or a diamond mine that will make me Tich I will not be particular if you call it a backyard or what you call it. That argument has been made by a great many persons. The states of Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Nebraska, Kansas, Missouri and the other western and middle western states were once in the same way the backyard of the Atlantic manufacturing states of the American union. But while they were in the same sense the backyard of the manufacturing states of the union they grew farm products which they shipped and sold to the manufacturipg states (of the union, and with what result? While they were thus the backyard of the manufacturing states of the union, the land in these states to which I have referred, which was wrorth $5 or $6 per acre forty or fifty years ago, is worth to-day $100 or $200 an acre simply for agricultural purposes. You may call the western plains of Canada, you may call the farms of Quebec, of Ontario, of the maritime provinces, backyards if you like, but if you can make the value of these backyards $100 or $200 per acre for growing food products that shall be sent to the very same markets to which these western states that I have spoken of have sold their farm products, if the result will be the same-and who will say that it will not be-then I say that the backyard argument has no force at all. Sir, I have said that these states of Illinois, Indiana, and other western and middle western states became prosperous and their lands increased in value while they grew food products for the manufacturing states. But while they were growing these, food products they became manufacturing states as well, and they built up within their territory such cities as the very city mentioned by the hon. member for Brandon, the city of Chicago, a great manufacturing city, St. Paul, Minneapolis, Omaha, and all the other large manufacturing cities that are now situated in _what was once a purely agricultural district of the United States. The same thing will be true of the western plains of Canada, and the same thing will be true, even more largely than it is true to-day, that as the farmers of the several provinces of Canada prosper, grow wealthy and add to the value of their soil, by cultivation, as their prosperity increases, as the value of their property increases, and as the population of these districts increase they will build up flourishing manufacturing cities and centres. and will not deserve, as they do not

now deserve, the term of backyard to the United States.
I am told that under this agreement the railway interests will suffer. Well, Sir, I take it that the railways of Canada were built for men, and not men for the railways. If either has to suffer, Canadian railways or Canadian men, then I liefer to let the railways suffer, but I do not think there is any evidence at all that the Canadian railways, upon which vc have spent a great deal of money, which have done a useful woik for Canada, and which are doing it well, will suffer as a result of this agreement. My hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely), in a speech which he made in this House, pointed to the fact, as other hon. gentlemen have since done, that the Canadian Pacific Railway stock is soaring to-day, that Canadian Pacific railway is worth $25 per share more than it was when we began to discuss this resolution. What does that mean? It means that Canadian business men, that United States business men, that the business men of the British Empire and the business men of Holland, in all of which countries Canadian Pacific Railway stock is held, have not one single bit of confidence in that argument, and do not attach any importance to the statement that Canadian railway interests will suffer by this proposal. My hon. friend from South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) quoted the opinion of Sir Donald Mann as to the effect of it upon the large railway line in which he is interested. We have had a woeful letter from Sir William Van Home.

I have referred to the dcleful letter of Sir Wm. Van Horne, and in contradistinction to that let me quote what was said by Mr. Thomas Skinner, the English director of the Canadian Pacific railway, as published in the Montreal ' Gazette ' of the 4th of February:
Thomas Skinner, the English director of the Canadian Pacific railway, in an interview confesses that he views the agreement with mixed feelings. If ratified, he said, the -agreement would have a disturbing effect on the Transcontinental railway, but the growth and development of the northwestern provinces of Canada were so great and rapid that he had no misgivings that this would more than meet the change arising from the agreement. On the whole, Mr. Skinner thonght this agreement advantageous to Canada, and though politically somewhat dangerous he was perfectly confident of Canada's loyalty to the -mother country.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
Hill was speaking a few months ago as to the present condition of United States railways, and he said it would take an immediate cash expenditure of six billion dollars to put the American railways in such shape as that they could prpperly carry the traffic there is for them to carry. And such will be the condition of Canadian railways. As Mr. Skinner has said, with the development of our western country, all our present existing railways would be overtaxed and we would have to have new railway lines. It has been urged by some, and I think it was stated in the letter of Sir Wm. Van Horne, that Mr. Hill's roads have now their noses resting on the international boundary line ready to cross into Canada and take Canadian trade to the south. But I would ask Sir Wm. Van Horne at how many places does the Canadian Pacific railway cross the international tine for the purpose of carrying trade from Canada into the United States? Hon. members on the other side, and opponents of this measure in the country have a great deal of concern as to our natural resources. The member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says:
That is the policy shining out in every line and article of this proposed agreement. The United States knows what it is after. With a tariff wall against the world, desiring to preserve its own unused natural resources so far as it oan, dipping into the natural resources of Canada so far as it may be able to, fortifying itself by the conservation of its own and by the destruction of ours, making itself -the great manufacturing country of the world and increasing its wealth and its power in that way.
Sir, the hon. member for North Toronto was wise enough not to argue that we in Canada have any control whatever over the United States tariff. Fcr many years rough sawn lumber has been admitted free of duty from the United States into Canada, and I do not know that we ever had a custom tariff on lumber entering this Dominion. Every member of this House must realize that the United States have quite as good a right to place lumber on their free list as we have to keep it on our free list, and if the United States have the right to place lumber on their free list then they have the right to place on that free list

every other natural product rve have in Canada. But the member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) made this argument. He said:
If this, agreement goes into force, a year from now this government may find, and the Conservation Commission may advise this government that certain of our natural resources should not be exported except under such and such conditions, or that they ought not to be exported at all, or that such of them as are made should be made under regulations and made in this country alone. As we are now we have a perfect right, to pass that legislation; we have given bonds to nobody.
That is a perfectly fair statement of the case; that while this parliament has no right whatever to interfere with the tariff of the United States we have the power, and if we choose to exercise it the right to impose export duties or to prevent or impede export of any of our natural resources. But while we have that power and right I will ask the member for North Toronto and every other member on that side of the House whether they think they would now, or in one year, or fifty years hence, advise the Canadian government to take that action. Sir, that is a game at which two can play. I do not think it wise for us to provoke such a war as that. If the government of the United States, of their own initiative, should prevent the export of their raw products it would be our part as men to meet them and checkmate them, and act as independently as they; but, Sir, the United States are not making any attempt to pass any such legislation, or to in any such way restrict the export of their natural resources. I have quoted from the work of Prof. Van Heiss on the conservation of the natural resources of the United States, and in that work he advises that it might be best for the United States to prohibit the export of many of their minerals especially, and other of their raw materials. And what would be the consequence? As I go through my own province of Ontario I find Ontario builders using Georgia pine. I have no doubt we could get along without that particular kind of lumber, but our builders use it because they find it convenient and profitable to use it. Canadian furniture manufacturers use large quantities of oak imported from the United States and not grown in Canada.
Last summer I was at Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, in the very large works of the Iron and Steel Company there. I saw their vessels bringing in United 'States ore which they mixed with Canadian ore to produce a better product. Their vessels were also bringing in immense quantities of United States coal, not obtainable in Ontario. How would this company, paying wages to many hundreds of workmen in Ontario, and other Mr. MILLER.
similar Canadian concerns, exist with the United States prohibiting the export of its raw products? I go through the cement factories in the province of Ontario and I find them using United States coal and United States coke. I ask the members of this House who have knowledge of the sub-,ieet how they think these Ontario cement companies could continue their business if they were deprived of the use of that coal and coke? In different parts of Canada there are large cotton factories, and we cannot grow cotton in any part of Canada, and if the United States prohibited the export of cotton these mills would have to shut down. Last night my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Lloyd Harris) said it ought not to be the policy of Canada to permit the export of unfinished products, but here are several instances in which the United States does permit the export from its territory to ours of raw products, so that we may make the finished article. Also, in the case of imported corn from the United States; the hon. member (Mr. Lloyd Harris) would not permit the Canadian farmer to sell his low grade wheat or barley, but would compel him, by legislation, to feed it to his stock on the farm. But the Canadian farmer to-day is importing corn grown in the States, just because the Canadian farmer finds it many times the cheapest food he can feed to his animals. The natural resource of which we are in the greatest danger of being deprived is our timber, and I would call attention to the fact that in 1899, three years after the Laurier administration assumed the care of the business affairs of Canada, they established a forestry branch, and through our Canadian forestry branch we are now encouraging the planting and preventing the annual loss of more timber than we are likely each year to export to the United States. Let me point to another contradiction in the speech of the hon. member to whom I have so often referred. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), after pointing out that the Canadian government is thus encouraging the depleting of our national resources, then argues that the United States would have reduced their tariff any way whether we had taken any action or not. He says:
That insurgent force that swept the Republicans out of power was pledged to a diminution of the tariff especially on food stuffs. The Republican party in that position, the Democratic party were pledged to a revision downward of the tariff especially on food stuffs. It was known by all men that the coming Congress soon to go into power would deal with that matter and it was known that it would deal with it in the line of taking off and diminishing duties especially upon natural resources and food stuffs. No one csn deny that.
If no one can deny that, and no one has denied that the United States would have

so reduced or taken off the duties, then how can any man blame this government for what it is said the United States would have done anyway? I do not know whether the United States would or would not have done so, but that is the argument that is made by our friends on the other side and they cannot argue along both lines. We have heard a good deal of the word trustees and our friends opposite have argued that we, the people of this day, and especially the government of this day are the trustees for the Canadian people, and that as trustees we ought to preserve to the people of Canada the natural resources of our own Dominion. Sir, if we are trustees in 1911 for the people who shall live in Canada a thousand years from now, was not the hon. member for Korth Toronto equally a trustee of the Canadian people in 1891, was not Sir John Macdonald equally a trustee of the Canadian people in 1891, and was not Sir John Macdonald equally a trustee of the Canadian people in 1871, when he proposed just such an agreement as this? And Sir, will it make any difference to the people who live in Canada one thousand years from now whether such a bargain as this was made in 1911 or in 1891?
I have -spoken of members blaming the government. It is the business of the opposition to blame the government, and they are very diligent in exercising that function. The leader of the opposition, in the speech which he made on the 26th of January, blamed the government, and particularly the Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Customs, for what he termed their surrender last year, in 1910. The language of the leader of the opposition was as follows :
The negotiations, in short, (that is the negotiations of this date) are a sequel to the surrender which this government made last year. I am, at the same time, of the opinion that if they had resisted firmly the government of the United States would never have imposed this maximum tariff against Canada.
That is the opinion of the leader of the opposition. It is the opinion of a political partisan, as we are all political partisans. If I expressed a contrary opinion that would also be the opinion of a partisan. But as to the negotiations in question let me quote the opinion of a man who is not a partisan; I refer to a work recently published by Professor T. W. Taussig, Henry Lee, professor of economics in Harward University, entitled: ' The Tariff History of the United States '. Professor Taussig, speaking of these very negotiations, says:
Negotiations with Germany and France led to some relaxations of their duties and regulations as to American products; and, in true mercantile spirit, these were held forth as great gains to American industry, and inferentially as causes of detriment to the foreign countries concerned. Negotiations with Canada led to but the slightest concessions. That country refused, as already stated, to modify her regulations as to wood pulp, or to make any changes of moment in her general tariff system. Some minor changes were secured, which enabled the administration to make a respectable show of having gained something in the way of lower duties; and a tariff war, which at one time seemed probable, was averted.
The statement of Professor Taussig exactly agrees with the statement of the Minister of Finance that President Taft was friendly to Canada, that he did not desire to impose the maximum tariff, that under the circumstances there was nothing else left for him to do, and that a tariff war was inevitable unless we afforded President Taft some shadow of an excuse that might enable him to avert that tariff war and by making slight concessions, termed by Professor Taussig minor concessions, we made changes that did no harm to any man in Canada, that did no good to any man in the United States, so far as the economic aspect was concerned, but that gave President Taft the excuse he desired to avert a tariff war, which I am sure every man in Canada, whatever his politics, would say, would have been unwise and would have been a calamity.
Now, Sir, I come to the attitude towards this proposal of our Canadian manufacturers. The manufacturers of Canada are making a very strong appeal to-day. They made a very strong appeal to Sir Wilfrid Laurier and we found that appeal in the Montreal ' Star ' a few weeks ago. That article which first appeared as a paid advertisement in the Montreal ' Star ' has since then appeared as a paid advertisement in many other newspapers. We have had articles in the Canadian ' Century ', and articles clipped from the Canadian ' Century ' have appeared in the local press from one end of this Dominion to the other, also as paid advertisements. The Toronto ' News ' has contained editorials and other articles in opposition to the treaty and let me read a part of a circular dated February 8, that was recently sent to an Ontario manufacturer from the office of the Toronto ' News: '
We are devoting considerable space daily, both in our news columns and editorially, to this question, and we have taken the liberty of placing your name on our mailing sheets for one month. No charge will he made for the paper, hut we hope you will be able to find time to read it each day.
I was lately in an Ontario factory, and in the office of that factory I saw several hundred pamphlets, neatly and attractively bound, containing speeches in opposition to this proposal, delivered by Mr. Russell. These were sent out by hundreds not only to this factory but, I suppose, to every factory in Canada for free distribution among the workmen in the factories. By these

means and by expending many, many thousands of dollars in printer's ink, and paid advertisements, the opponents of this proposed agreement have sought to create and have for a little while created a public opinion in opposition to this proposed arrangement. Let me say that this public opinion that has been created by the expending of so many dollars in printer's ink and newspaper advertising is but a temporary public opinion, it is frothy and on the surface and will not have any lasting effect in influencing the judgment of the Canadian people.
Nowr, Sir, I have not the slightest prejudice against Canadian manufacturers. We have in Canada great natural resources. We have great forest wealth, we have great mineral wealth, and there is no country in the world with greater water-powers. But we have something better than forests and mines and water-powers, we have men of manufacturing skill and ability, of business ability and of commercial enterprise. We have men of inventive genius, and,
I am glad to say, of large capital, and there is no reason why Canada should not become a great manufacturing nation. My hon. friend from Hastings (Mr. Northrup) I think it was, said yesterday that no one could intelligently argue this matter without putting the manufacturers on one side and the farmers on the other. In that I do not agree with him. In my opinion, if this arrangement will benefit the farmers, it will also benefit our manufacturers. I have no patience at all with those who call manufacturers thieves and robbers, who say that they are parasites preying upon the people. I respect a man, be he manufacturer or farmer, who is doing an honest day's work for an honest day's pay, and helping to build up this country. Some manufacturers are charged with being selfish and no doubt they are, just as are some of our farmers, and some of our members of parliament; and it may be that the manufacturers, through the manufacturers' association, occasionally give prominence to their selfish instinct. But while we require revenues for the building up of our great public enterprises-for the building of the Hudson Bay railway, the Georgian Bay canal, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Welland canal, for the extension and improvement of our rural postal system, for everything necessary to develop this great country-while we require revenues for these purposes, I believe it will be the will of the Canadian people, for many generations at least, that a large part of this money shall be raised by means of a customs duty. While this is the case, we ought to Tegulate our tariff and collect our duties in such a manner as will afford reasonable protection to the manufacturers and other industries throughout the limits Mr. MILLEE.
of our Dominion. But where or how, under this proposed arrangement are manufacturers hit? If I refer again to the Toronto ' News,' and its report of the speech of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sif-ton), and if I were to accept his statement, I might be led to conclude that our manufacturers are being hit. Well, I have great respect for the hon. gentleman, and that respect is not diminished because he has chosen to leave his party on this occasion. That is the right of every one sitting on either side of the House. I remember the time when, in his palmy days, the hon. gentleman had a good deal of influence in Canada; I remember when .the name of Sifton was one to conjure with, but I do not agree in everything he said a few evenings ago. I find in the Toronto ' News ' this quotatioin from his speech:
Let me enumerate what I think will be a few of those effects. Some industries will be destroyed, there can be no doubt about that. What reason can be given for drawing your pen through an item of the tariff and shutting up an industry which is not accused of combining as against consumers, which is not accused of charging illicit prices or of any other evils; what reason can there be for selecting that industry and wiping it out of existence I cannot see. I am bound to say that it does not appeal to my common sense.
In reply to this, I will say that had my hon. friend made his customary use of his common sense, he would not have indulged in any such language. He said that some industries will be destroyed. What industries? What reason had he for stating this? He asked what reason can be given for wiping an industry out of existence? Well, I cannot see that any industry will be wiped out of existence under this arrangement. What manufacturing or other industry will even have its profits lessened by this, proposed arrangement?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: What about the salt industry?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
That is not a fresh question nor is it a large industry. The manufacturers themselves do not go nearly so Ear as my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Sifton) did. I have referred to the appeal to Sir Wilfrid Laurier which appeared some time ago in the Montreal Star. In that appeal the ' Star ' says:
So they disarmed suspicion by not betrayin'* any great greed in 1 taking, and then deftly secured the assent of our representatives to a * gift ' of such far-reaching effects that it engulfs our commercial independence and endangers our national existence.
Thpn the 'Star' says in that appeal:
Oh! but the tariff on manufactured goods remains, it may be said, for the present it does.

The manufacturers therefore, admit that they have not been hurt and the tariff has not been changed in any way to do them injury. Evidently, the troubles that afflict our manufacturing friends are not real but imaginary. I do not believe that our Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has the slightest intention of making any bargain that will operate to the detriment of any manufacturing concern in this Dominion. I believe further that hon. members on this side would not support the government in any attempt to do material injury to Canadian manufacturers. In my opinion the manufacturers of Canada will be helped by this agreement. They will be helped in this way. As you help the farmers, as you more thickly populate our western country, as vou give the farmers better prices and better markets for this produce, you make them better purchasers of manufactured products. In helping the farmer, you enable him to buy more manufactured goods and of better quality and pay better prices.
My hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) referring to the American newspapers said:
To-day, when I read the American papers and scan the American speeches, and look at the American arguments, I do not find that they are saying very much as to the employment of American capital in the establishing of American industries in Canada. In the past and present condition of things we have noticed that as a factor, and a very important one, in the development of this country. It is stated, and I think without doubt, that at least $226,000,000 have been transferred in equipment and plant from factories in the United States towards the establishment of branch factories in the Dominion.
My hon. friend did not of course find it possible to read all the American newspapers, and I would draw his attention to the South Bend ' Tribune,' published in South Bend, Indiana, on the 30th of January last. This gives an account of an interview with Mr. Oliver, who is at the head of the largest plough works in the wide world:
According to Mr. Oliver, the reciprocity measure introduced in Congress last Thursday does not affect his concern to such an extent that he should show more than passing interest in the legislation and consequently the plans of the Oliver industry relative to Hamilton will not be changed in the slightest degree. Should the measure as now constituted become a law the duty on ploughs would be lessened only from two and one-half to five per cent, the intention being to reduce tbe tariff from 171 and 20 per cent to lb per cent. This charge it appears is too small to warrant the Olivers altering their plans at Hamilton
'The reciprocity treaty does not affect us,' said Mr. Oliver, 'and there is absolutely no truth sent out in the report from Ottawa
that we have ordered work stopped on our Hamilton plant. We will go ahead with all our plans in the spring and rush our factory to completion. The proposed change in the tariff on ploughs is so small as not to affect us.'

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
I agree with every member -of this House and every citizen of Canada that we like to see American capital brought in to establish industries in this country. But, if I am to make a choice as between a large factory built in Canada with United States capital, and a large factory built in Canada with Canadian capital, I will every time choose the latter. And why? Because every manufaicturing establishment is built to secure to the owners a net profit. In the case of a factory backed by American capital it is true, money from outside will be spent in erecting the building and paying wages, but the net profit from that American institution will be taken to the United States to further develop that country, while in the case of the factory built with Canadian capital, the net profit will remain in Canada foi the development of onr own country.
Sir, on a recent visit to my own Ontario town of Hanover, I found that the Knech-tel Furniture Co., was about to construct a new factory to build a new line of goods. I was informed also that the Spiesz Furniture Co. was preparing to build, next year, a large addition to its present works. The Hanover Specialty Works are making plans for a large extension of their plant. And it was rumoured on the street, whether truly or not, I do not know, that Mr. Ball, who was my opponent in the last election and will be my opponent in the next election should I run again, is intending to build next summer a large addition to his factory. In Neustadt, another town in my riding, six miles south of Hanover, a large chair factory that is in operation there intends to construct a large addition to its works. Also the Durham Furniture Co. in South Grey intend greatly extending their works next year. And this sort of thing is not confined to the towns of South Grey alone, but applies to every other manufacturing town in the province of Ontario.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: If I may be permitted, would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Miller) state whether the manufacturers he has referred to are in favour of this trade arrangement or not?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
I will come to that, and I will tell my hon. friend (Mr. Blain) exactly what they say about it, most of them. What does this development of manufac-

turers show? Whatever may be the effect upon United States (manufacturers, the Ontario manufacturers who fully understand the situation, a/re not alarmed by this agreement, nor do they believe that it will cripple their business or lessen their profits. But there are other factories in Canada that will be helped by this agreement. I refer to the barns, the stables and the silos of the Canadian farmers. I refer to the tile-draining that is to be put down by the Canadian farmers. I say that the Canadian farm is a Canadian manufactory and is manufacturing products that bring greater wealth to the Dominion than do even the products of the factories which we usually call factories.
Is it true that United States manufacturers are in doubt to-day about coming to Canada to start branch factories here? If they are timid, why are they timid? The blame is not to the government, the blame is not to the friends of this measure; but the blame is to the opponents of this measure who are creating a panic by their unfounded cries and unreasoning alarms; these are the men who are keeping American capitalists from investing their money in this country.
Speaking of the Oliver Plough Works brings me especially to the matte: of agricultural implements, concerning which we heard a great deal from the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Harris) last night. Now, I would like to know where our hon. friends on the other side really stand as to this matter of agricultural implements?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: Where do you stand on that question?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
I am always willing to tell the hon. member where I stand. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) speaking in this House on the 26th January, and referring to the' reductions proposed to be made on agricultural implements, said that he did not believe the change proposed would yield the slightest iota of relief to any farming population in this country. At that time, he appeared to think the occasion demanded relief, but said that the reduction of two and a half per cent and five per cent was not sufficient relief. I remember when, a couple of years ago, the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner), a Conservative, introduced a resolution in this House to reduce the tariff on agricultural implements to ten per cent. But my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who to-day tells us that a reduction of two and one half per cent and five per cent following a similar reduction made two or three years ago, will not give sufficient relief, when the hon. member for Souris, two years ago, moved his resolution to reduce the Mr. MILLER.
duty to 10 per cent, voted against that resolution. If he thinks two and half per cent to five per cent repeated is not sufficient reduction, and if be thought that the 10 per cent reduction proposed by the hon. member for Souris is too much, I would like to know where he stands.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: I would like to know how the hon. member himself voted on that resolution.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend (Mr. Bradbury) frankly that I voted the same w7ay as his leader (Mr. Borden, Halifax) did, and I would so vote again. If hon. members ask how I voted, and what I think of the duty. I reply that I think, exactly as the ' Farmers Advocate ' does upon this subject. The ' Farmers Advocate ' is, perhaps, the leading farm journal published in Canada. It welcomed some reduction in the duty on farm implements, but said in an article on this very subject:	It is hardly fair to single
out any one industry for 'Sacrifice. And with that I quite agree. I quite agree in the policy of a reasonable reduction, but I do not think it would be right to single out that interest and make a sacrifice of it. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Harris) last night, said:	If this government is to be opposed to manufacturing in Canada, I will have to remove myself from Canada.
Well, the hon. gentleman need not remove himself, even though the company to which he belonged a little while ago did remove a large part of its capital from Canada to the State of New York. The Massey-Harris Company, of which my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Harris), for whom I have great respect, is a member, has made a very large amount of money in manufacturing in Canada a very good class of agricultural implements. With the money they made from Canadian farmers they recently purchased in Batavia, New York, a plant that cost them, I think, something more than a million dollars- several millions, I am informed. That was before this proposal had been made, before my hon. friends the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs had gone to Washington, or had thought of going to Washington. I think that the government of Canada had a fair warrant and a good reason for making a slight reduction in the duty on agricultural implements when they saw the evidences that appeared about them on every hand. If a Brantford agricultural implement manufacturing concern can take its capital and compete in the United States against its United States rivals, without even one per cent of protection, surely they can compete, as Mr. Oliver says, they can in Canada, with a protection of fifteen per cent. Then let me

say that in the very city from which the hon. member for Brantford comes, the Cockshutt firm, manufacturing ploughs, have for some time been sending Canadian ploughs into the United States and Selling them at a profit in large numbers, in spite of the duty they have to pay.
Sir, I do not know where the opposition stands in the matter of agricultural implements and the duty thereon. I do know what the government has done. The government reduced the duty from two and a half to five per cent two or three years ago, and they have reduced the duty again this year, or will by this proposal, a further two and a half to five per cent. If any one were to ask me what is the position of the Hon. Mr. Borden on this question I would say: Well, I do not know. If a manufacturer asked me if I thought that Mr. Borden would be an advocate of a greater reduction, I would say: Well, by his speeches in the House I would think that he would. But if a farmer should ask me what Mr. Borden would have done, I would say: Well, by the vote he gave upon the resolution of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, I would think that he would be opposed to any reduction. I do not know, I am sure, where he is, because he seems to speak in one way and vote another.
Let me now touch upon the question of loyalty. The poet Cowper, in his poem, I believe it is in ' The Task,' says :
Patriots ,are grown too shrewd to he sincere,
And we too wise to trust them.
Dr. Johnston said:	'Patriotism is the
last refuge of a scoundrel.' Sir, I do not believe that all are insincere scoundrels, who, in this day, are crying loyalty and waving the flag, but some of them are. I say there are men who are loyal to-day for financial gain, that there are other men to-day who are loyal for political profit and advantage, and I say further, that there is another class of men who are loyal to-day, really and sincerely loyal, but who are nervous and frightened by the panic that our friends of the opposition endeavour to create. I say further that he who will readily wave his country's flag for material gain, or for political advantage, will not always be the last to trample it in the dust for a like consideration. Let us not make too cheap the flag for which our fathers fought, some of them, and for which we would be willing to fight again. We are all loyal on both sides of the House, Grits and Tories in Canada are loyal, and let us not talk or speak otherwise. Sir, the agriculturists in Canada-and my hon. friend from Lambton, if he were here, would agree with this-know that some years ago the British government imposed on Canadian cattle what is called the embargo. We
know that the British government years ago. by that embargo, barred out live cattle. They did it to protect their own agriculturists, and they maintained it to protect the British farmer and the British breeder of livestock. Sir, we do not quarrel with them; we do not say that the people of Britain are not loyal because they do that; but we do say that if the government of Britain seeks to protect its cattle raisers and cattle breeders by imposing and maintaining that embargo, they are far too fair and generous, and far too sensible, to blame the Canadian government for endeavouring to protect the interests of Canadian farmers as they do under this agreement. My hon. friend opposite asked me about the manufacturers in my own town. Let me read him a letter from a German Canadian manufacturer in the riding of North Waterloo. This man says:
I still have confidence that the future of this great country of ours is safe in the hands of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his followers at Ottawa, and I believe the Liberals of North Waterloo-which is a large manufacturing district-'feel the same as I do, that the reciprocity agreement with the United States will be a good thing for Canada as a whole. I do not for a moment believe in the blue ruin cry, and that Canada, by entering into a freer trade arrangement with our cousins to the south of us, will in the end become part of that country. The German-Canadians of North Waterloo will remain loyal to the British Empire no matter if we have free trade with the United States or a high tariff wall. Annexation has nothing whatever to do with this undertaking.
Sir, I commend these -words of a German Canadian, whose fathers and forefathers spoke not the English language; I commend the loyalty of this German C.anadian to my friends of the opposition, of British parentage, whose fathers came from the old land. The letter of this German Canadian expresses, I believe, the sentiments and the feelings of German Canadians generally. and I say that the loyalty of this German puts to shame the fears and anxieties of our British Canadian friends on the other side of this House. I see before me on the opposition benches men who are engaged in agriculture, men who are engaged in businesses of different kinds, and I ask if there is one of them who will to-day admit and confess that if he sella in the United States market an article for which he can find there a higher price than he could anywhere else, will that make him less loyal? Will it make him feel like severing the ties that bind him to the British flag? If any hon. gentleman opposite can purchase an article he desires in the United States market to better advantage than he can purchase it in any other market, will it make him less loyal? If there is such a member on the opposite benches, I would like him to stand up for

a moment that we may gaze upon him, and see what manner of man he is. Not one Conservative in this House, not one opponent of this agreement in this House, will make any such admission as that. I say ask them how these men dare to insult the people they represent, how they dare insult the people of their constituencies, by thinking for a moment, by saying with their tongue, that the men whom they represent are less loyal than they themselves?
Sir, I say that this trade arrangement will help the farmers of Canada, and with this argument I close my speech. The opponents of this measure say that the hon. the Minister of Finance and the hon. the Minister of Customs ought to have shown in greater detail what will be the results of the working out of this proposed agreement. It is impossible to give statistics that any one can say will turn out to be correct, because this agreement will affect different parts of Canada in different ways, and it will affect Canada differently in different years and under different circumstances. We are like a man whois looking out for an opening for his business. He goes to a place where everything would indicate that there is a good opening. He cannot tell what his first year's sales will be, and what his second year's sales will be; but he says: The conditions appear to be good, and I know that I can do a good business here, and here is where I am going to locate.
Now I know that the hon. member for North Toronto, when he was Finance Minister entertained the House and the country oftentimes with very neatly compiled and tabulated figures which he called statistics. They might better oftentimes have been called guesses and my hon. friend was frequently a bad guesser. My hon. friends opposite, say that this agreement will not benefit the farmers, but I say, Sir, that it is worth noting that there is not a Canadian farm paper published in any province in Canada that is devoted to the interests of agriculture, that as not upholding this agreement, and is not in favour of its being completed. The hon. member for St. Antoine, Montreal (Mr. Ames) says that you cannot protect the manufacturers of this country and not protect the farmers, that if you do not protect the farmers, they will demand, and you will have to yield to their demand, that every vestige of protection be taken from the manufacturer." I can understand that you can protect the Canadian manufacturer to some extent and to a great extent, it may be, but I say that a protective tariff upon food stuff would be just as much _use to the Canadian farmer as a coon skin coat would be to the hon. membeT for St. An-Mr. MILLER,.
toine on a July day with the thermometer at a hundred in the shade.
This agreement will give to the Canadian farmer additional markets. It will not deprive him of one single market that he has to-day. We grant subsidies to-day to steamship lines running to every distant part of the globe, and if we do all that, surely we cannot justify it and refuse to make every effort to trade with our nearest neighbours. Let me read to you- and I will not weary you with long figures -a statement of the subsidies we are paying to-day to assist steamship lines Tunning to these several different countries:

Making a total in steamship subsidies to countries other than Great Britain of $843,475 a year. In addition to these annual subsidies to steamship lines, we have trade commissioners in the Argentine Republic, Australia, British West Indies, China, Cuba, France, Germany, Holland, Japan, Mexico, Newfoundland, New Zealand, and South Africa and Canadian commercial agents in Jamaica, Trinidad, Bahamas, Colombia and Norway. In addition to paying the salaries of these trade commissioners and commercial agents and the expenses of their offices, we also, through the Department of Agriculture, maintain at very great expense, Canadian exhibits wherever there is a large world exhibition in any part of the globe. We have had exhibits in Japan, Belgium, Italy, Scotland and other countries. Not one single member of this House has made any objection to the payment of these steamship subsidies, not one member of this House has made any objection to the establishing of these commercial agencies, not one member of this House has made any objection to the expenditure for the making of Canadian exhibits. The hon. member for Brandon was a member of Sir Wilfrid Laurier's cabinet when these steamship subsidies were agTeed to, when these paid agencies were established, and yet the hon. member for Brandon, while he was a cabinet minister and since he was a cabinet minister, has made no ob-

jection whatever to any of these expenditures. Now, Sir, if it be common sense, if it be good business to pay out these tremendous sums of money for steamship subsidies, for trade agencies and to maintain Canadian exhibits in different parts of the world, why in the name of common sense is it not good business, is it not good economy, is it not good politics, to make every possible effort, although without that large expenditure, to trade with our nearest neighbours, especially as our nearest neighbours are a very populous and wealthy people, who can afford to buy and pay good prices for that which we produce and that which we have to sell?
I have said that this agreement will benefit the farmers. My hon. friends opposite endeavoured to make a point against my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) yesterday, by saying that he had referred to the grain growers and the fruit growers of Canada as wolves. He did nothing of the kind. Sir, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister saw wolves nearer to him than the fruit growers or the grain growers of the west. He saw wolves sitting on the opposition benches and their wails and cries and how-lings have been heard now for many, many weeks.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: A few over there, too.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
Well no, there are no wolves, but	there are for the moment, some two or three sheep in wolves' clothing. 1 have said that the proposed trade arrangement will increase the price of wheat to the farmer in the west. That has been denied and it has been argued the other way. A few years ago a personal friend of mine, who was in the employ of the Customs Department, had just come down from doing duty along the southern line of Saskatchewan and the international line between Manitoba and the United States. That gentleman told me when he came back to Ontario, that a great many Canadian farmers living near enough to the American line, were smuggling their wheat from Canada, and selling it.to the United States elevators in Dakota. Why? -not because the price of wheat was quoted higher on the American market than on the Canadian, but because dishonest Canadian elevator men were falsely grading their wheat and the Canadian prairie farmer was obliged to sell wheat that was really No. 1 at the price of No. 2 or 3 because it was given a lower grade by the elevator man, while by smuggling his wheat across the line the Canadian,, farmer escaped the false grading and got 10 or 12 cents a bushel more for his wheat on
the American side than he could get on the Canadian side. I leave it to hon'. members from the west to say whether or not this practice has been pursued by the elevator combine.
The hon. member for St. Antoine, Montreal, said that this agreement would destroy the identity of our exports. It will not destroy the identity of our exports. The hon. member for St. Antoine, Montreal, is a manufacturer of boots and shoes. He knows that there are some men, whether they are right or wrong, who prefer an American shoe to a Canadian shoe, but they will not buy an American shoe, simply because they know it is an American shoe. They realize that there are good American shoes and there are very inferior American shoes. The Canadian buyer, who wants an American shoe, wants one with a brand or name on, that he knows is the brand or name of a superior shoe. So, if any of my friends desire a bottle of English pickles, it will not be enough to know that it is an English pickle; they want to know if it has the label of Crosse & Blackwell, which is an assurance that it is a superior article. The Canadian shipper of superior Canadian product gets a good price in the British market, because of the individual brand that his produce bears when he exports it.
It is said that this arrangement will destroy the market of the Ontario and Quebec horse breeder in the Canadian west. Well, I do not believe that. At present, and may be for a few years to come, the Ontario and Quebec horse breeders will have a market in the Canadian west, but how long will that continue? We know there is no country in the world better adapted for the raising of horses than the prairies of the west, and we know that the farmers there are paying a great deal of attention to the industry, and it will only be a few years when the Canadian west will have horses to sell rather than horses to buy. And then, how important will it be to the horse breeders of Ontario and Quebec, and of Canada generally to have the advantage of the tremendous markets afforded by the large cities of the United States. This arrangement will benefit the raiser of Canadian cattle and Canadian lambs. It will also benefit the man who raises barley in Canada. The hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) and the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Lloyd Harris) told us that the Canadian farmer ought not to sell his barley and low grade wheat, but rather feed it to his stock. Well, while these two gentlemen may be good business men and while the one may be a clever manufacturer and the other a clever lawyer, I think it would be better for them not to oblige the Canadian farmer by legislation to do anything he does not wish to do writh the pro-

duce he raiseg. I think we may give the Canadian farmer credit for having enough intelligence to know whether it would be better for him to sell his grain or to feed it.
I would remind these two hon. gentlemen that possibly the Canadian farmer would have enough business ability and intelligence to realize that it is to his profit to sell his barley, and to buy American corn with the money he gets, and feed his animals just as well with the com, and have a good cash balance left in his pockets besides. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) spoke of the purchase by Canada of United States cheese, and he pointed out that Canada buys cheese from Britain and some of the countries of continental Europe, but the hon. gentleman knows that the cheese bought by Canada is not similar to the cheese that Canada produces.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: I do not know anything of the king, and neither do you.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
If my lion.- friend (Mr. Taylor) will go to the dinner table of the House of Commons restaurant and ask for some of the cheese of continental Europe he will learn something that for many years he has neglected to learn. A prominent business man of Brockville told me the other day that a farmer of the county of Leeds came to his office and said: I have been all my life a Conservative, but do you see yonder across the St. Lawrence river the American town of Morristown, from that town runs a cold storage train every day down to New York city and that train carries cheese, and butter, and milk, and cream, fruit, and meat. All the products of my farm would be worth more money to me loaded on that cold storage train (if there were no duty in the way) than they would be in any part of the world. And this farmer said:	Sir
Edmund Walker through his banking institution may take in hundreds of thousands of dollars of the hard earned money of the farmers and other toilers of Canada, and upon one-third of it pay no interest, and on the other two-thirds pay three per cent interest, and he can take that money down to the same city of New York and lend it to United States stock speculators at the rate of 25 cents per annum, so that his banking institution may pay a dividend of 16 per cent per year, and Sir Edmund Walker will still be a loyal Canadian and lecture me upon my lack of loyalty, but if I send a calf across the St. Lawrence river and sell it in Morristown for $6 more than I can get for it in Brockville I am accused of disrupting the British Empire.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext: Name that gentleman.
