But taking the quotation as correct, all I can say is that the comment made by Mr. Turner in London was what one would expect under the circumstances. Mr. Turner was representing British Columbia, and he felt that it would not be fitting for him to state that the fruit industry of that province was not able to compete with that industry in any other part of the globe, so he endeavoured to make the best of the situation. But looking after the files of the standard of empire, I found another opinion of our agent general in London, and this is what he said in effect:
There is not the slightest doubt that the ultimate effect wiill be to divert the great bulk of Canada's food supplies to the United States, and that he believes that the preferential soheme, as outlined by Mr. Chamberlain, is the only possible way to overcome the serious effect of the new agreement on Canadian relations with the mother country.
It is my intention very briefly to discuss what, in my opinion, are some of the reasons which have brought about this ill-considered, unexpected and almost complete reversal of the fiscal policy of Canada, which we have had during the past 45 years. It is true that from time to time there have been requests for readjustment



came to the parting of the ways, and with your permission I would go back and review one or two other incidents in order that you may better understand the attitude of the two' parties. In 1870 when the question of taking British Columbia into the confederation arose in order that we might have this outport on the Pacific which some men to-day are endeavouring to force into a closer relationship with the nation to the souths the same men then said that the cost of securing the trade of British Columbia for Canada would be too great, that the province was not worth it. British Columbia was then separated from the rest of the confederation by at least two thousand miles of unknown territory, then, largely a wilderness. There were a few isolated settlements here and there along the Red river. There was between the east and west the Rocky Mountain range. On the Pacific coast there were a few settlements. One of the conditions under which British Columbia agreed to enter into the confederation was the building of a transcontinental railway. It was absolutely essential, if she was to trade with the rest of Canada, that that undertaking should be completed. When the hon. the Minister of Mines (Mr. Templeman) was speaking the other day, almost his first words were that he remembered the time when there was no trade east and west with the province of British Columbia, but when all the trade-* all the trade,' and he repeated it-was north and south, and he seemed to be proud of it. Well, Sir, there were men in those days as there are men to-day, who were turning away from the promised land, and looking back [DOT] to the flesh pots of Egypt, men who preferred to trade north and south rather than east and west. There were men in those days, on that side of the House, who said the task was too great for the people of Canada to undertake. They said:	Even though we
succeed in this vast undertaking the results will not be worth the while. They said British Columbia was nothing but a sea of mountains.
But, Sir, we are glad to say that the same spirit of Anglo-Saxonism, the same spirit of British statesmanship, that animated the Liberal-Conservative party of that day when they gathered together to bring about confederation, that same spirit animates the Liberal Conservative party to-day. The building of that road was indeed a huge and difficult task. You must remember that not only had we to build the road, but we had first to take population into that wilderness before any natural products could be secured to bring out on the road. But there were men then, as there are now, who were ready to undertake the task; they knew that if they sowed in the evening they Mr. GOODEVE.
would reap a harvest in the morning. But there were other men who said: You have burdened this country with an enormous debt, you are assuming large obligations, but you are not getting the results which you expected. And so we find these same hon. gentlemen to-day, opposite always ready to complain, always ready to find fault. But at the same time we find also the broad-minded men of Canada coming to the fore. Now the time came that one of those crises that come to all nations, came to Canada, as it has come to every nation in the world, when there was a world-wide depression in trade, when we found our farmers working unprofitably early and late, when we found these scattered villages along the frontier of this enormous territory for four thousand miles, when we found many of our mechanics without work. Then the same men who were trying to build up Canada stepped into the breach and they said:	If we are
to become successful in building up a nation we must round out the country, we must build up our industries and our factories; and so they fought the great fight we are fighting to-day, and they adopted the principle of a National Policy. How did they do it? By one or two men in a dogmatic way bringing down a resolution and asking this House to support it, without consulting the people at all? No, but they formulated a National Policy, which was discussed" freely and frankly in the House; it was discussed on every platform in Canada, it was discussed in every news paper in Canada, and finally they issued a manifesto to the people of Canada, relying on their sound sense and good judgment, and the result was that they were returned to power on the great question of a National Policy. Sir, that day there came a change into the affairs of this great Dominion of ours. The small and scattered villages lying along our shores grew from villages into towns, and from towns into cities. Everywhere we saw the smoke and steam of industry and heard the sound of the hammer. We gradually evolved a home market for our people, and those farmers who heretofore had been complaining, and justly so, of lack of a market commenced to ' sell their home products to the artisans, labourers and mechanics in these growing towns. The result is that gradually but steadily they removed the mortgages from their farms and there grew up confidence in the power of the people of Canada. They felt that this was the policy for them, that no longer would they look to the nation of the south, that they were able, as their fathers had been before them, as the great pioneers and colonizers of the world, to build up their own national life and so they continued along that line.

Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I had briefly traced the history of this country from tfle date of the union of the scattered provinces under one political constitution. I had mentioned the taking in of the outposts on the Pacific coast and the binding together of these provinces from Nova Scotia to Vancouver by a great transcontinental railway. In each of the three great crises of our history since then there rose up broad-minded Canadians, men who put principles above partyism, men who were prepared to sever their party ties and affiliations in order that they might do what they believed to be in the best interests of true Canadian nationalism. I am glad to learn that at the present hour, when we have arrived at another crisis in our history, there are still great Canadians, men in all walks of life, who are prepared to look on this question from a broad national standpoint, men who are prepared to absolve themselves from their party allegiance to further what they believe to be the welfare of our country. I have said that I would deal with this question from the point of view of the statement made by the President of the United States, and in order that we may understand what President Taft meant by that statement I shall read it, with its context, and I shall also read the opinions of other men who are in a position to speak on this subject. President Taft said:
The identity of interests of two peoples linked together by race, language, political institutions and geographical proximity offers the foundation. The Dominion has greatly prospered; it has an active, aggressive and intelligent people. They are coming to the parting of the ways. They must r-con decide whether they are to regard themselves as isolated permanently from our markets by a perpetual wall or whether we ore to be commercial friends.
In connection with those words of the president in his message, let me read the opinions of others who are in a position to interpret the meaning of these words and the meaning of this reciprocity pact with the United States. Mr. McCall, Chairman of the Ways and Means Committee of the House of Representatives, said:
The benefits to us would he enormous, if we could sweep away all tariffs between the two countries. It would have the effect ou our trade of another Louisiana purchase.

Fifty years hence the population of the United States will probably be 200,000,000 and the American people will cross the border in steadily increasing numbers, so that the population of the Dominion is likely to be made up largely of Americans, possibly a majority, and who can tell what may come through the friendly relationship with the mothc :[DOT] country of both the United States and Canada? There is another opinion as to what this reciprocity treaty will lead to. I will now quote a man, who, under the peculiar constitution of the United States, occupies an almost similar position to that of the Premier of Canada. I refer to the Speaker of the new House of Representatives, Mr. Champ Clarke. It is true that Mr. Clarke has been cited before, but we cannot impress on the minds of the people of Canada too often what he says was intended by this reciprocity pact. Mr. Clarke spoke, not in a joking way, I assure you, but as a shrewd, capable, careful legislator, a man who occupies the highest position in the American Congress:
I look forward to the time when the American flag will fly over every square foot of British North America up to the North Pole. The people of Canada are of our blood and our language. If the treaty of 1854 never had been abrogated, our countries would be much further advanced than now towards this end.
In that particular I agree with Mr. Champ Clarke, and you will remember that I have already said that in my opinion the abolition of that treaty was a blessing in disguise and has done much towards the upbuilding of the great country we have to-day. Mr. Martin, of South Dakota, interrupted and said:
Will the gentleman favour the abrogation of our tariff law entirely so far as Canada is concerned, and make free trade on all products?
Mr. Clarke-By taking Canada in to become a part of the United States-Yes.
Then Mr. Norris, of Nebraska, asked:	As
I understand it, the gentleman favours the Bill for at least one reason, that it will have a tendency in the end to bring Canada into the union?
Mr. Clarke replied-Yes, I have no doubt about that.
Now mark, the statement is here made that he favoured the Bill for one reason, Mr. GOODEVE.
and what is the one all-compelling reason that influences this man, who occupies such a high position in the United States, viz., to bring Canada into the American Union? His one all-prevailing reason is that it will have a tendency to, in the end, bring Canada into the American Union. Now, Mr. Chairman, if that should be the result of this treaty, and honestly and sincerely I fear that is its tendency, then I would like to ask every Canadian throughout the Dominion if they are in favour of such a thing? In that connection I would like to cite a statement which has not yet been published, and which should have the greatest possible weight with this government, with the Finance Minister, and with the Minister of Customs. It is the statement of a man who was a Liberal and a free trader, a man who did more than any one man in the great British Empire for the building up of that empire, a man who almost unaided and alone has brought an entire Dominion under the Union Jack. I refer to the late Cecil J. Rhodes, of South Africa. The words of Mr. Rhodes are almost prophetic. When I read them a few months ago I never expected they would apply as they do on the present occasion; I never looked forward to the time, and I hoped I never should see it, when these words would have the bearing on our country's position that this pact gives to them. Dear Sir,-I wish to write and congratulate you on winning the elections in Canada. I read your manifesto, and I could understand the issue. If I might express a wish, it would be that we couid meet before stern fate claims us. 1 might write pages, but I feel I know you and your politics as if we had been friends for years.
The whole thing lies in the question:
And note this:
Can we invent some tie with our mother country that will prevent separation? It must he a practical one, for future generations will not be horn in England. The curse is that English politicians cannot see the future. They think they will always be the manufacturing mart of the world, hut do not understand what protection coupled with reciprocal relations means. I have taken the liberty of writing to yon, and if you honour me with an answer I will write again.

It is a marvellous thing and it appealed to me as a young Canadian. Fancy those prophetic words, and think of a man who has done so much for the empire. He asks! Can we invent some tie with our motheT country that will prevent separation; it must be a practical one. Now take the explanation given by Rhodes himself of what he meant by a practical one. He says

that he is both a free trader and a Liberal and he presses this not only in his words but in the message he gives. He says he is inclosing a cheque for £5,000 to assist the Liberals in the election at that particular time. He says further:
The labour question is an important one, hut deeper than the labour question is that of the market for the products of labour, and as your local productions can only support about six millions of people, the balance depends upon the trade of the world	
If you had had statesmen you would at the present moment be commercially at war with the United States, and would have boycotted their raw products until they came to their senses.
I ask the House, is that not a marvellous prophetic utterance. He says:
If you had had statesmen yon would have boycotted their raw products until they came to their senses, and I say this because I am a free trader.
Later on he says:
I.am horrified by Morley's speech on Egypt
You know what that speech was, Morley was willing to let Egypt go, he was not willing to shoulder the burdens of the empire. And see what this great statesman says:
If you think your party hopeless, keep the money, but give it to some charity you approve ef. It would he an awful thing to give my money to breaking up the empire.
Mr. Chairman, I fear, and I say it in all sincerity, that we have reached that jioint to-night that was certainly the position when the commercial war was brought on in 1891. This letter was written in the fiscal year 1891 and those were the words of this statesman. He made these remarks after discussing 'the whole question, he feared it might mean the breaking up of the empire and he said: It would be an awful thing if I should be a party to the breaking up of the empire.
I appeal to yon and to every member of this House having the interest of Canada at heart, looking back at her history for the last 150 years, realizing the difficulties we have come through, that we should he careful before casting our vote on a question of this nature. Who of us has not -stood on the ocean shore? We have watched the waves as they come and go, coming in nearer, nearer and again receding and it has been difficult for us to say at times whether the water was rising or receding. Thus it has been with the history of Canada. There have been times in the history of Canada wheq the tide of trade, the tide of commerce and the tide of prosperity has risen and come near, and again there have -been times of trade depression when the tide seemed to recede, and finally,
like these waves of the ocean, have come in those mighty waves of prosperity until we of all nations of the world have been prosperous. Our banks, our saving banks, our trade, our commerce, our workmen, out artisans, everybody has been successful and prosperous and just when this tide of prosperity is at its very height, like a bolt from the blue, without mandate, without consultation with the people, without consideration of the requirements of .this country of ours, without asking or seeking that they might be guided in this great undertaking, in the reversal of this policy, they have cast this holt, upseting, endangering and interfering unless we check it now, retarding the wonderful development that we have made up to the present time.
I have endeavoured very broadly to lay down the foundations from which we are to discuss this question, and I would like to discuss one or two _ of its economic phases'. Before I do so, will you permit me to puncture three or four of the free trade air bubbles of my hon. friend from Red Deer? The first argument he advanced will he found at page 4239 of 'Hansard.' When he was describing the wonderful prosperity and progress of the manufacturers of Great Britain, he took as his best illustration of that progress the great manufacturing establishment of Lever Brothers, the head of the Sunlight Soap works. He said they had built up such a great industry in this line that it was one of the largest in the world, and he attributed that result to free trade; but he ended by saying that they had branch factories in the "United States, in Germany, in France, in Switzerland, in Belgium, in Australia and in Canada. Did the hon. member stop to say why they have factories in all these highly protected countries? Would they have built a branch factory in Canada had it not been for the duty and the protective tariff on soaps in this country? That little factory here in Canada to distribute this great product employs several hundred hands, who in turn make a home market for the very agriculturists to whom my friends were referring. We have the home market of the masons, the bricklayers, the carpenters, who erected these buildings. We have the home market of the mechanics, who built and installed the machinery in that factory. Carried to its logical conclusion, all of that trade, all of that home market would be still in Great Britain had it not been for the protective policy adopted in Canada in 1878. What would we have had? The farmers for whom he was speaking, would have simply had the price of their wheat less the_.cost of carrying in competition with the surplus wheat of the entire world and the British

workmen would have formed the home market for the products of the British agriculturists and thus we break the first free trade bubble of my hon. friend.
I now come to the second argument. He referred to intensive farming. He referred many times according to the habit of hon. gentlemen opposite, to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster). I find, however, that they invariably - fail to answer the arguments advanced by that hon. gentleman, and it was so in this case.
Here is what he says at page 4240 of ' Hansard: '
Intensive farming was subject which I had hardly expected to hear my hon. friend from North Toronto growing eloquent upon. He did, however, seem to hint that intensive farming would be hurt by this reciprocity arrangement. He did not give any facts to support that idea.
Then he goes on to quote Cobden as usual, and he ends iip as follows:
In free trade Britain to-day-if I am wrong, the Minister of Agriculture will correct me -33 bushels of wheat to the acre are grown on the average; in protected America the average is 14 bushels to the acre, and in Canada, with our virgin soil, it is only 17 bushels. What is the matter. I ask my protectionist friends, with little Britain as a country where intensive farming is carried on under free trade?
And my hon. friends opposite actually cheered him. I would ask any man is there absolutely .any argument in all this, anything but a mere statement of fact, a mere statement of the fact that in Dakota they raise 14 bushels of wheat to the acre, and in our Canadian Northwest 17 bushels to the acre' while in Great Britain they raise 33 bushels per acre? But let me give the argument which my hon. friend failed to make. If there be any logical deduction to be made from these facts it is this. It is that the Dakota farmer has robbed his soil of its fertility and destroyed its value and that the Canadian farmer in our Northwest is rapidly following in his footsteps, whereas the farmers of Great Britain, by keeping their by-products at home and feeding them to their stock, have enriched and increased a hundred-fold the value of their land. That was the argument made by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), and that is the argument which my free trade friend (Mr. Clarke) failed to see. And so I have pricked another of these airy bubbles.
But a little later at page 4246 of ' Hansard ' my hon. friend said:
This empire has grown up on the basis of absolute freedom of its component parts. Would you have us repeat the experiment that Great Britain tried with her American colonies and which lost them to the empire? Was it not this very mistake of mixing up Mr. GOODEVE.
trade relations with politics? Was it not that which led George Washington

My hon. friend is fond of quoting Cobden and these other men who are long past and gone.
*-to advise his countrymen so earnestly not to become entangled with the politics of foreign nations? Now, the rule in Britain is to make her own tariffs, and what is good for Britain is good enough for Canada.
And again we heard the cheers of my hon. friends opposite. Why, if there is anything in it, that is the very argument we have been endeavouring to put forth on this side of the House ever since the day this proposed treaty was brought down. We have been urging that we should make our own tariff, free from the politics of the United States, free from their influence, and free from any complications with that country which must eventually lead to trouble and disorder.	.
Again we break the third bubble of my hon. friend the free trader.
As a fourth argument he said:
What are tbe facts? Mr. Cobden, in a speech which he delivered after the repeal of the corn laws, drew attention to the fact that the most notable thing after the repeal of tho-e laws was the improvement of agriculture in Great Britain.
Well, it is one thing to make an assertion and another to prove it. Let us see if there was any improvement in agriculture in Great Britain. I have here extracts from an expert report on the agricultural conditions in Great Britain. They are in newspaper form and not tabulated, but I shall give some of the results:
In 1873 Great Britain had 3,670,259 acres under wheat. Whereas in 1908 she had only 1,664,860 acres under wheat. During the same period her acreage under barley has shrunk by 750,119 acres; that under beans has shrunk by 401,203 acres; that under peas has decreased by 156,824 acres; that under potatoes has declined by 264,598 acres; that under turnips has shrunk by 641,850 acres.
During the last fifty years the number of agricultural labourers in the United Kingdom has decreased by more than a million.
Ireland's acreage under wheat has shrunk from 743,871 acres in 1847 to 43,600 acres in 1909. Ireland's agricultural labourers decree sed from 850,100 in 1851 to 212,200 in 1901.
The agricultural area of Germany is only about one-third larger than is the agriculture area of the United Kingdom. Yet for every single sack of bread corn, produced in Great Britain, Germany produces ten sacks for every ton of potatoes produced in Great Britain, Germany raises seven tons; for every pig raised in Great Britain Germany raises six pigs. Free trade has ruined the agriculture of Great Britain and especially that of Ireland.
Free Trade Accused.
Since the introduction of free trade, about twelve million British people, a population

larger than that of Scotland, Ireland and Wales combined, have left the United Kingdom. Tho population of Ireland, which came to almost nine millions when free trade was introduced in 1846, has declined to about 4,300,009 at the present moment. Many of the British manufacturing industries have experienced a similar decline. Between 1851 and 1904 the workers employed in the British silk industries have decreased from 130,723 to 30,184.
And note this:
On the other hand in the United States, under protection the workers employed in the silk tiade have increased from 1,723 in 1850 t>
79,601 in 1905.
Thus in the United States, under its high protective system which my hon. friend so strongly condemns, the silk industry made marvellous progress. This was a new industry in the United States. Britain had had a long start, Britain had her silk mills well established and was supplying the markets of the world, yet the workers employed in the British silk industries had decreased from 130,000 to 30,000. On the other hand the workers in the silk mills in the United States had increased in numbers from 1,743 in 1850 to 79,601 in 1906. I do not think I need labour that argument any further. These are authentic statistics showing the results of free trade in Great Britain; and as one hon. member on the other side pointed out the other evening, there is probably no country in the world where there are more people living upon charity than in the United Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland.
I want to' give another evidence to my hon. friend because I want to prove very fully this particular argument I am making:
A Gratifying Comparison.
In ten years from 1898 to 1908, the commerce of Canada has increased 88-14 per cent, and that is a greater increase than any other country in the world with the exception of the Argentine Republic, which shows an increase of 164 per cent. The increase in the commerce of the United States for the same period was 55-19 per cent, while that of Great Britain was 37-81 per cent.
I think that is a conclusive proof that the bubble I have referred to, bubble No. 4, is completely exploded.
He made one other argument, and it also was based on what had been said by my hon. friend from North Toronto. He made quite a pretty figure on the ' preference wax doll.' Well, the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) has so effectually melted this wax doll that therf is not even the smell left-so it is not ne cessary to deal with that argument fur ther. Having dealt with the only pointf he has made, I will now leave him in his lonely furrow, and pass on to the hon
member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell). That hon. gentleman went out of his way to scold the banks for paying the farmers only three per cent interest, forgetting that this was brought about by the government he supports reducing the interest paid in the government savings banks on July 1st, 1897, from 34 per cent to 3 per cent. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) quoted many statistics in regard to his own province. But, when questioned by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) he did not seem to be quite sure of what his statistics meant. I would only remark to the hon. member for Carleton that I know of no two things on which so many false doctrines are built up as the misuse of statistics and the misuse of the scriptures. Let me give one illustration. The hon. gentleman took the trade returns in potatoes, which, he said, was one of the important points-and hon. members will recollect that I pointed out that the hon. Minister of Finance had brought back free potatoes for the maritime provinces. And, after quoting certain figures, the hon. member for Carleton said,
' This is a complete history from the Canadian standpoint, of the exportation of potatoes to the United States up to 1910.' Now, I took the trouble to hunt up the figures of the imports of potatoes into Canada from the United States for six of the years covered by the quotation of the hon. member for Carleton. In his discussion of the matter, the hon. gentleman said that there had been only one year during his lifetime when potatoes had been lower in the United States than in the maritime provinces. Now, I have put the figures as given by the hon. member and printed in ' Hansard ' alongside the figures of the Trade and Navigation Returns showing the imports of potatoes for these six years. And I find the remarkable fact that, for four of the years that the hon. gentleman himself selected, we imported more potatoes into the Dominion of Canada than we exported. In other words, we are throwing open the market of Canada to the United States, and no doubt the whole country will realize before they get through with it that this Canadian market in agricultural products has been exposed to competition from every agricultural country in the world. What does this prove? It proves simply the doctrine we laid down in the beginning: that there are bound to be times, along the border of four thousand miles long, when their local fluctuations will cause the advantage to be now on this side and now on that. What, then, is the argument that follows? Why, it is that we must deal with these questions from the broad national standpoint, considering, not local conditions, but the good of Canada as a whole. It is absurd to deal with a question of this nature along narrow lines. The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) read to-day in this House a statement which completely refuted the allegations with regard to the prices of butter and other agricultural products. I intend to deal with that more fully a little later on. In dealing with this question of the importation into Canada of agricultural products from the United States, I would like to quote a gentleman who, in 1903, was secretary of the Minnesota branch of the National Reciprocity League. He made an exhaustive study as an expert on behalf of this league, taking evidence on the whole question. Let me give some of the facts he gathered:
Our farmers should understand that in opening; up our markets to Canada's natural products, we are also getting a big markot there for our natural products. We hear very much about how the agreement is inimical to the interests of the barley raisers, but our attention has not been called to the fact that last year we exported 164,000 bushels of barley to Canada and paid thereon a duty of 15 cents a bushel. Canada removes this duty under agreement. Last year our farmers shipped 7,680 tons of hay to Canada

This is the very argument the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) was trying to make this afternoon, and here is the expert answer:
-and somebody paid a duty of $15,360 on that hay. Last year Canada bought 215,000 bushels of potatoes from us, and a duty of $13,000 was paid thereon. Of other fresh vegetables, Canada bought from us last year $652,000 worth, and had to pay on them tariff taxes of $195,000. Of apples alone

This is another argument of my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B.:
-Canada bought last year from us 59,071 barrels, and the duty thereon was $24,000.
These apples will come in absolutely free under this arrangement, and then where will this market be to which my hon. friend refers?
Canada bought from us last year several thousand head of cattle, 121,000 horses, 104,000 sheep and 24,000 other live animals', and a vast quantity of poultry, the total duties levied on which amounted to $175,000. All of these now go on the free list, and the Canadian market for them is to be as nn-Mr. GOODEVE.
trammelled as the market in any part of the United States.
While meats are not placed on the free list, the reductions offered by Canada are so sweeping that there must inevitably be an immense increase in our exports of such products to Canada,
Then he goes on giving statistics. We have had so many statistics read in this House that I dislike to weary the House by reading any more; yet it is necessary to do so in order to make clear our arguments. He says:	'
What this means to our market for meats can be inferred from the fact that last year the imports of these articles from the United States into Canada wore so enormous that the total duty collected by the Canadian government amounted to more than $600,000. The amount of the duty Canada remits on these products-based on last year's figures-will be almost $400,000. Last year Canada imported 750,000 dozen eggs from the United States, and paid a duty of $23,000 thereon. Eggs go on the free list now.
So I could go on all through the list of agricultural imports into Canada. Thus we see how strongly this arrangement is going to work against the interests of the agricultural classes of Canada. Now let me for a moment refer to the trip west of the right hon. the leader of the government. He spoke at Nelson, British Columbia, in the district of Kootenay, my constituency, and was reported in the Daily ' News '. Speaking of myself he said:	' He is a
Tory, that is all the reproach I have to make against him, but it is a very serious reproach Well, I am glad I do not look upon it as such. He went on to say:
May I be pardoned if I go one step farther and say that in other respects the people of this section of British Columbia did not consult their best interests. Why how old is this city? Ten, fifteen years at most. This town ®>wes its existence largely and its prosperity certainly to the policy of the government, which by the grace of God and the will of the Canadian people has been at the head of affairs for the last fourteen years at Ottawa. How so? Well sir, three things have characterized the policy of this government. Transportation, immigration and their fiscal policy. In all these things I claim that the policy of the government has largely contributed, not only to the existence but still more to the prosperity of this city and all the cities of the Kootenay valley.
Here the leader of the government makes the claim of building up all the cities of the province of British Columbia. He also claims credit for his fiscal polity. Now, I want to show the right hon. gentleman what the people of Nelson think of this marvellous fiscal policy of his, which he claims has built up the entire province of British Columbia. The night this treaty was announced by the press despatches, the people of Nelson, not waiting to write, realiz-

ing the gravity of the situation as it would affect that district, immediately called a meeting of all classes of the community, regardless of politics. The fruit growers of that district met and passed this resolution, which they sent by telegram:
A meeting of fruit growers this district here to-day, following resolution unanimously passed: Whereas the fruit growers of the Kootenay have invested heavily in developing orchards, relying upon the government of Canada to maintain existing tariff conditions as affecting their products, or in case of any modification affecting fruit to benefit to an equal rate by modification of the tariff on other articles affecting the cost of production of fruit; and, whereas the cost of production in this district is increased by the fact that labour and all supplies are higher by reason of a generally productive tariff and of the distance from eastern Canadian manufacturing centres than it would otherwise be; and, whereas, the industry being as yet in the early stages of development in this district, the costs are higher than in the older established districts in Washington and Oregon, from where the fruit comes into competition with ours, while there is nothing in the proposed reciprocal arrangement to reduce the cost of production; and, whereas, the proposed reciprocity arrangement with tile United States would remove the protection which we now enjoy and would doubtless lower the net profit (taking as an instance on our apples by the amount of the present duty, viz., 13 cents per box); and, whereas, our orchards have been planted with varieties more suitable to the Canadian markets, which are our best market, under our tariff system, and it would be impossible for us to take advantage of the market for special varieties of fruit in the eastern cities of the United States which would be opened to ns by the reciprocity arrangement, without in most cases sacrificing existing orchards and developing new ones; and, whereas, we do wot consider it wise or safe to develop orchards requiring years of labour and large expenditure, depending upon a condition which might be terminated at any time by a foreign power; and, whereas

Now note this, because I consider it is an absolutely proper and common sense way of looking at the question. This is not a pro forma resolution passed to bolster up the government, it is a declaration of men whose very bread and butter are at stake. And what do they say:
-there is no compensating benefit to ns in the proposed reciprocity arrangement, and the result will be injurious and unjust to us; therefore, be it resolved that we, the fruit growers of the Kootenay in mass meeting assembled, do protest against the proposed reciprocity arrangement as regards fruit being put into force, and do respectfully request the government of Canada not to make such reciprocal arrangements regarding fruit at this time.
Have wired this to Minister of Customs, kindly hand on our behalf copies to Finance Minister, Senators Templeman and Bcrstock and Burrell; other resolutions by mail.
I immediately had copies of this resolution made and forwarded to the parties mentioned, from whom 1 received replies saying they had received it. Now, Sir, look for a moment at this remarkable situation. These men, whose means of livelihood were absolutely threatened, wired down to their representative, as they had a just right to do, asking me to endeavour to protect their interests. And what was the result? Why, if I am to take the answer of the leader of the government to the fruit growers of Niagara district; 'It is too late'. Did you ever hear of such a thing, Mr. Chairman, at any time of your life? I ask you if that is a constitutional method of procedure? No one can be heard. Who are the people of this country? They are not the government. As I said before, the government stands for the whole people, it means the people in this democratic country of ours, and- no two men. and no set of men, have any right to put the country into this position. Having forwarded their message to the gentlemen they mentioned, I was forced to write back to them: ' I am utterly helpless in the situation '. I appeal to you, I appeal to any one in this House, if that is a democratic form of government. Now we have two additional resolutions which were forwarded to me by mail, and here is one:
Moved by N. Wolverton, seconded by C. F. McHardy,		
Whereas various fruit pests exist m the United States of which we are fortunately free, and,	.
Whereas the diseased and hence inferior fruit from the United States is our worst competitor,
Therefore he it resolved that this assembly of fruit growers of the Kootenays earnestly petition for such a rigid inspection of imported fruit as exclude all defective fruit.
Now let me explain that to the Minister of Finance who negotiated this treaty. We have in the province of British Columbia fruit inspectors on whom we spend large sums of money annually. I have seen in my own town, box after box of apples that came from Washington and Oregon, burnt by the fruit inspector because of their diseased condition. This is what makes every British Columbian proud of the fruit industry of that province, the superior quality of our fruit to that grown south of the line. I myself have walked, ridden and driven hundreds of miles through the beautiful valleys in the very district here referred to. The Prime Minister himself went through that region, and in beautiful language described its beauties and wonders. Yet he comes down here, and with one fell blow is about to destroy the livelihood of those people.
What is the position? I have gone there and I have driven through those remarkable orchards. One thing that strikes a man from the older settled parts of Can-

ada or the United States is the absolute freedom from disease of our fruit there. It is marvellous to see the thin skin of the fruit. Any man who has been accustomed to the older orchards will be immediately struck with the marvellous freedom from disease of any kind when he sees the pear, plum or apple trees there. The skin of the peaches is absolutely transparent, the fruit is perfect to look upon, and yet I regret to think that fruit is to be allowed to go and come by the removal of this tariff. I see my friends smiling. Of course, we can continue to have our inspectors there and we shall continue to have them, but I say that it is the part of this Dominion government to assist us with regard to that question. Now, Sir, I would like to read another resolution passed by a board of trade-a public, non-political body -with regard to the efiect of this treaty. In passing, let me say that it is a remarkable thing that the Minister of Inland Revenue, in reading those resolutions in favour of this proposal, which he had to admit, in answer to a question from this side of the House, were all from Liberal associations, failed to read this resolution. We have been inquiring day after day and the government are failing to bring down information with regard to the other side of the question.

Then, I will gladly apologize to the Minister of Finance, because I wish to make no unfair statements My hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) informs me that the resolution was brought down two days ago, although it was received over a month ago. Now, I will read the resolution of the Nelson Board of Trade:
Moved by F. A. Starkey, seconded by W. B. Farris, that in the opinion of this meeting the proposed reciprocal tariff between Canada and the United States is one of the most important questions that has come before the people of Canada, and in view of the fact that British Columbia has the prospects of great future industries in fruit-growing, min-Mr. GOODEVE
ing and lumbering and that sufficient time has not been given the people of this province to carefully consider all phases of this great question and they are not in a position to know what effect such a tariff would have on the industries of British Columbia, therefore, the government should give further time to the consideration of this question, and that a special investigation should be made as to the effect that this tariff, if passed, will have upon the future development of British Columbia. Carried.
I would like to know how hon. gentlemen feel with regard to the resolution they voted down yesterday in which wre asked, in the very language of this resolution, for more time to consider the question. I have anotheT resolution which was wired to me by the Creston Board of Trade. Creston, in my opinion, is quite equal to the celebrated Okanagan Valley. It is at the head of Kootenay lake and they have made a wonderful success of the cultivation of fruit at that place. I know in one instance personal to myself, of a man who squatted there without a dollar and who took off, in 1908, $1,275 per acre in strawberries and, in 1909, $1,400 per acre. I think this is one of the best parts of British Columbia. Here is a resolution from their Board of Trade:
Creston, B.C., Feb. 2, 1911.
A. S. Goodeve, M.P., Ottawa,-Following resolution passed by this Board. Kindly pass on to Messi's. Burrell and Bostock: Whereas proposed reciprocity agreement introduced by Sfi. Fielding will inflict severe blow to fruit and lumbering interests of province without giving any equivalent, and whereas the fruit industry is in its infancy and requires fostering, and whereas fostering these industries of vital importance to welfare province, and whereas proposed agreement would imperil capital investment of those interested in this industry, now be it resolved that this Board strongly condemn proposed agreement as far as applied these industries.

speechtext:
I have here a personal letter from a fruit grower, Michael Phillips. He sends me a long letter in which he sets forth similar reasons why this proposal should not be adopted. I have also a resolution from the Victoria Incorporated Co-operative Fruit Growers' Association, Limited, which reads as follows:
That we, the directors of the Victoria Incorporated Co-operative Fruit Growers Association, Limited, hereby view with alarm the contemplated removal of the duty on American fruits, as explained in the daily press, under the proposed reciprocity agreement between the Canadian and American governments, and believe that such abolition of the tariff on fruits will greatly retard and depreciate, if not utterly destroy, the fruitgrowing industry in British Columbia.
I have a similar resolution from the Central Farmers' Institute, a public non-political body representing the whole province,

the resolution having been sent here by the deputy minister of the province. It is as follows:
Resolved, that the Central Farmers' Institute views with- alarm a movement recently advanced by the grain growers of the prairies for reciprocity in natural products with the United States, as such an adjustment of the tariff would be of material disadvantage to the horticultural industry of this province, and this meeting is strongly of the opinion that not only should no reduction of duty on fruit be permitted by the Dominion government, but that immediate steps should be taken to place our duty on a parity with that of the United States, wihiioh in several instances is considerably higher on various kinds of fruit than ours.
Further resolved, that a copy of this resolution he sent to the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the lion. Minister of Customs, the hon. Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. R. L. Borden, and the several representatives of British Columbia and constituencies in the Dominion House of Commons and members of the Senate from this province. Carried.
I have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant,
W-M. E. SCOTT, Deputy Minister.
I have also a resolution which I think has already been put in by my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo, from Nanaimo. Now then, I just wish to say a word or two, because this aspect of the question has been fully and fairly dealt with by my hon. friend from Yale-Cariboo. The right hon. leader of the government took credit for building up and developing this particular district; yet, by the carrying on of this pact they will retard to a very great extent its further development. I do not wish to be placed on record as saying that we will be utterly ruined, because I believe that the free spirit of these western Anglo-Saxon people will rise above every difficulty and obstruction, but I do claim that the Dominion government should not do anything that will retard in the slightest degree the development of this great industry in that district.
That particular district needs special nursing, for the reason that these are small valleys scattered along a series of very beautiful lakes, and there being the difficulty of getting a very large acreage in one district the transportation problem becomes acute. There is also the fact to be found in all new countries that it is difficult for the people to get together to find a particular kind of fruit that is best located for a particular district, and along that line the provincial government is spending a large sum of money. They have established numerous experimental stations which become necessary because the conditions of soil and climate vary "very materially within a short distance owing to air currents and the influence of
the varying altitudes. All these are difficulties which icall for special sympathy, special aid, and special assistance but instead of rendering us that sympathy we have received no consideration from this government. I shall not labour that argument because it is very ably presented to the House by my colleague (Mr. Burrell), and I shall briefly sum up the reasons against this arrangement, taking as my basis the many resolutions that have been received, which on examination will be found to be not exaggerated in any way.
This arrangement will be most detrimental to the agricultural Interests of our province, and will be a disastrous blow to the fruit growing industry if carried into effect.
1. The result of prices obtained by fruit growers for the past four year's crop has shown very small profit over the cost of production, owning to keen competition from the American States. 2. Western American growers can secure their labour for orchard work fully 25 to 30 per cent cheaper. The cost of material, fruit boxes, wrapping paper, &c., is quite 25 per cent cheaper in the American States. 3. The cost of production of a box of apples to the grower in the foregoing States is approximately 40 cents. It costs the British Columbia grower, owing to the causes advanced, from 60 to 65 cents. 4. The present duty on a box of apples is 13 cents. It will thus be seen that the duty as now imposed is not nearly sufficient to compensate for the cheaper labour and material which the Americans have. 5. By the removal of duty imposed on American fruit entering Canada under present conditions, the American States will be able to undersell British Columbia in the markets of the middle west, as also in the home market. 6. Large sums of money have been invested by land and irrigation companies and private individuals in developing the fruit industry of the province, and their interests should be protected. 7. The provincial government has spent a considerable amount of money in recent years in ' advertising the fruit growing possibilities of the province, and have thereby attracted men with capital who have planted out lairge areas in fruit. 8. If the proposed tariff agreement becomes effective, a cheek will be put on men with capital coming to our province, thereby materially retarding the exploitation of our agricultural and fruit lands. '9. We have been struggling during the past ten years under somewhat adverse and difficult circumstances to develop our fruit industry, thereby bringing a yearly increasing revenue to the province. Abolition of the duty at present imposed means fiercer competition from the American States and we receive in return absolutely no

equivalent advantage. 10. The great fruit growing districts of the interior, wheire fruit growing has been made a speciality, will receive a serious setback if the present duties are abolished, and this will result in a lowering of land prices all round. 11. Men who have settled in ouir lands, putting labour and capital into them, and thereby developing our agricultural resources, should be protected. 12. The problem in British Columbia at the present time is that of settling our lands, and thus developing our agricultural and fruit industries. Too much of what should be produced in the province is imported from the United States, and this is increasing each year. Any course of action such as the proposed tariff agreement, which will discourage land settlement, is against the interests of the province, and should be strongly opposed. 13. An agreement which has been advanced by those in favour of a free interchange with the States, is that British Columbia will secure cheaper fruit, and that it will not interfere with provincial grown fruit. This is not correct, as our principal competitors are the States of California, Oregon and Washington, whose fruit comes into the market practically at the same time. As a matter of fact, it comes into the market shortly beforehand, and this consequently lowers the price for British Columbia fruit arriving immediately after. 14. It will divert interprovincial trade between the eastern provinces of Canada and British Columbia to the States, thus sending money to the American side which, as loyal Canadians, we would wish to see stay in our great Dominion. 15. It will materially affect traffic on our own transcontinental lines, by diverting a portion of such traffic to foreign railways. 16. It will be a setback to imperial preference, and federation of the empire which we all, as component parts of the greatest empire the world has ever seen, look forward to in the near future. 17. It is altogether a one-sided arrangement. Wre gain practically nothing, and lose much. 18. Let well alone. Our Dominion, and British Columbia in particular are entering on an area of unprecedented prosperity. Capital to develop our great natural resources is pouring into the country. The tide of immigration has set our way, and under existing conditions our future is assured.
The following figures furnished by the Inspector of Fruit Pests regarding imports into the city of Vancouver, are interesting. There were 79,388 boxes of apples imported; 14,367 of pears; 14,186 of plums; 655 boxes of prunes; 64,702 boxes of peaches; 12,699 of apricots; 473 boxes of crabapples; 25 boxes of quinces, and 11 of nectarines. These amounts would represent 206 full carloads of fruit of ten tons each. When you con-Mr. GOODEVE.
sider the other cities of the coast, and the interior, one realizes what a very large amount of fruit crosses the American side into our local markets. The present proportion of fruit marketed by British Columbia in the middle west does not reach 25 per cent of the total amount sold there.
Now, just a citation from the budget speech of the Minister of Finance of the province of British Columbia which was submitted to the legislature a few days ago. It will be interesting to every member of this House, as it is to every Canadian who is interested in the. development of our western provinces. It is rather a remarkable statement. I may say that the Minister of Finance in introducing this subject gave the source from which he took his figures and like our own Minister of Finance he explained that it was difficult to get statistics of that nature bearing on agricultural products, but he took his information from the railroads and the express companies, and he had his figures rechecked, and he says he thinks he can safely say that they are at least approximately accurate. The provincial Minister of Finance finds that for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1910, British Columbia produced $14,399,000 worth of agricultural products and there were imported into that province $14,962,904 worth of the same products. It will be noted that the province imported approximately the same amount as she produced. Now I appeal to every member of this House, and particularly to the members from Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. We have here an interprovincial trade with British Columbia of over $14,000,000 consisting of horses, cattle, sheep, swine, poultry, butter, cheese, milk, bacon, meat, lard, pork, fruits, vegetables, eggs, honey, hay and grain; all of which can be raised in the -western prairie provinces, and can be exchanged for the fruit of the province of British. Columbia, because as we know the prairie provinces do not produce fruit. And yet at one stroke this interprovincial trade will be very materially injured if not practically ruined, temporarily at any rate. So much for the local side of that question.	_
Thus far I have been dealing rather with the sins of commission of this government, and if they have done many things that they ought not to have done I may say that they have also left undone many things that they ought to have done. When the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs were down at Washington, did it not occur to them that there was something else they might have offered from the province of British Columbia in exchange for this free fish instead of our fruit industry? It did not occur to them that last year, in this House, we very properly voted $50,000 for experimental purposes to discover a way of treating the zinc ores of that province. Did they not realize, be-

cause they have the statistics, or could get them from the Minister of Mines, of the enormous value of those zinc ores in British Columbia, what it would mean to the Dominion of Canada if we had a successful treatment of those ores? They must have known, or should have known, before going into a question of this kind, of. what immense value that would have been to this great district, with its newly developed, complex, mixed lead and zinc ores. Yet I find no reference in this treaty to these ores. Under the Dingley tariff ore was admitted free to the United States, but under the Payne-Aldrich treaty of 1909 the duty on mixed zinc and lead ores carrying over 25 per cent of zinc was one cent per pound on the zinc contained in the ore. There were certain reductions from this on ores carrying less than 25 per cent of zinc. As a matter of fact, the class of ores we have in that province are such that we could not export any that did not carry the amount set forth, so for practical purposes on all we can export the duty will be one cent a pound under the Payne-Aldrich tariff. In consequence of that, we deal only with that duty. The reason given for the imposition of this tax under the Payne-Aldrich tariff was that they were in competition with the zinc ores of Mexico, where they had low-priced coolie labour, and that this was being done on behalf of the American miner. I would call the attention of the minister to the way in which the Americans guard the interests of their miners, their workmen, their artisans and mechanics. The reason advanced did not apply in any particular to the province of British Columbia, because, as I will show you, not only do we pay as high wages as the Americans, but better wages. The British Columbia miner receives 50 cents to a dollar a day more in the zinc districts than the miners receive in the zinc districts of the United States. This refers to New Jersey, Missouri and Wisconsin. It is to be noted that considerably more than two-thirds of the zinc in the United States comes from New Jersey, Missouri and Wisconsin, and in none of these states are the wages paid as high as in British Columbia. The 'Engineering and Mining Journal' of January 11, 1911, page 25, says that the wages of miners in Wisconsin were $2.50 a day, and of muckers $2 a day. The muckers in British Columbia get $3 a day of 8 hours. It is necessary for the Canadian producers to sell their zinc ores in the United States, or ship them to the United States for smelting in bond for sale in Europe: there is no other way in which we can treat one pound of those zinc ores. So they are absolutely lying idle. If the Minister of Customs was in his place I would call his attention to an argument he made in this House, when he said: Do the people of Frontenac county want their iron
ores, forsooth, to remain in the ground, because, possibly, at some future time their great-great-grandchildren might take them out? Let me give him his answer back and ask him: Do the people of British Columbia want their zinc ores to lie idle in the ground, because, possibly, their great-great-grandchildren may take them out? Yet neither hon. minister gave any attention to this great industry. The production of zinc ores in the United States, Mexico and Canada has been as follows:
1906.	1907.	1908.	1909.Tons.	Tons,	Tons.	Tons.United States.. Mexico 	
Brit. Columbia.	905,000 89,000 600	903.000 109.000 1,100	838,000 66,000 6,100	1,000,000 100,000 10,000
We produced these amounts notwithstanding the fact that we have to fight against this duty and to go to foreign zinc smelters to have our ores treated, to send them through in bond, and to pay all expenses and send them to the European market. Did it not occur to either minister that they might fairly and justly ask the United States in adjusting their tariff to remove that duty? The Americans themselves now want it removed, and I feel satisfied that if the ministers had merely suggested it it would have been done at once. The unpopularity of the zinc tariff in the United States is shown by the following comment of the ' Engineering and Mining Journal' of January 7, 1911:
The results of 1910 showed that the tariff on zinc ore has not benefited the miners, the prices of zinc and zinc ore having averaged no higher than formerly, while it harassed the smelters. Thus it has helped nobody and has hurt somebody.
There is this difference in regard to lead. The government of Canada gave a bounty of $5,000,000, and very properly so, as they did in the steel bounties, and if it were not for that bounty, under the conditions we have in the United States, it would be impossible to operate our lead mines. As a matter of fact, a very large proportion of the zinic mines we cannot operate at all for the reasons I have stated. That is one of the sins of omission, and so it is in regard to this whole question. The more we see of it the more we find that they seem to have given it little attention and not to have studied it in all its relations. I would like even now, under the circumstances I have placed before the minister, to see the minister endeavour in some way, without putting it into this compact, if they are bound to force it through, that
*

some arrangement is made whereby that duty could be removed from the zinc orej of Canada. The smelters themselves on the other side, as set forth by the ' Mining and Engineering Journal,' are quite prepared to bring their influence to bear in that direction.
A word in regard to lumber. Let me say frankly it is a difficult question to deal with, or to argue about. You see the difficulties here. Our government had already removed the duty on lumber, and the result is that our markets, particularly our western prairie markets, have been flooded with the surplus products of rough lumber of the western United States. I was talking to a lumberman in this House to-day, and any lumberman will tell you that there is invariably a surplus of rough lumber at any mill. It is like the rough meat. The packers will tell you to-day that the reason of the high prise of meats is because they can only sell the choice cuts. It is the same with the lumber industry. The Americans had plenty of rough lumber, which it was often difficult to dispose of, and whenever there was a glut in their own market they dumped it into the prairie provinces of our northwest. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) knows that delegation after delegation of lumbermen brought pressure on the government to have a duty put on, but he said thev could not do it in the interests of the prairie provinces. Well, I am not here to discuss that question, but I am only saying that the supposed advantage given by the Americans in taking the duty off lumber is of no benefit so far as British Columbia is concerned. The Americans always have plenty of rough lumber, and it is impossible to send ours into their market and compete with it.

speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell the House who took the duty off rough lumber?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
The Conservative gov. ernment took it off in the interests of the prairie provinces when the settlers came into these provinces in the early days. At that time the great spruce areas in that district north of Edmonton had not been opened up; at that time we had not developed the lumber industry in British Columbia to the same extent as to-day. Neither had we the same transportation facilities, and so the Liberal-Conservative . government, as it has always done in dealing with these tariff questions, took off the duty in the interests of the people at large.
Let me now give you an extract from a letter written by Sir William Van Horne. In that letter he quotes what Senator Beveridge said with regard to the point I have made. Sir Wm. Van Horne quotes Senator Beveridge as saying:

speechtext: What is the name of that gentleman?

speechtext:
I think that is an entirely private matter but the hon. gentleman can take my word. I would be very glad however to give him the name person-nally after the adjournment. I may say, however, that he is a gentleman who I am sure would command the respect and confidence of my hon. friend.
I have here a photograph which I would like the House to see in connection with a letter sent to the Minister of Finance by the Western Canada Bag, Envelope and Box Board Company, to protest against this proposed arrangement. This is a picture of a new building in the process of
erection in the constituency represented by my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Taylor) for making coarse paper, roofing paper, felts, box boards, &c. In their letter they say:
If the reciprocity agreement, so far as it pertains to building paper, roofing paper, sheathing, &c., is adopted as proposed, it will positively kill this industry and prevent the operation of the plant.
Here is a letter which they sent me to show the impossible position in which they will be placed:
I take the liberty of enclosing herewith a copy of letter which we have just forwarded to the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in reference to the removal of the duty on building, roofing and sheathing paper, deadening felt, carpet lining, box board, &c. We are also pleased to enclose herewith a photo taken sometime ago of our plant which is now under course of erection at New Westminster and which we wish again to emphasize we will be unable to operate if the proposed reciprocity agreement is adopted.
A copy of that was sent to the minister, and here is the letter to the Prime Minister himself:
The Honourable Sir Wilfrid Laurier,
Premier of Canada,
Ottawa, Ont.
Honourable Sir,-In reference to the communication which we addressed to you under date of February 9, protesting against the removal of the duty on building paper, roofing paper, 6heathing, deadening felt, box board, &e., we wish to say that- the removal of the duty on the above products will have such a vital and disastrous effect upon our industry, that we take the liberty of suggesting, that if in your opinion you deem it advisable, we shall be pleased to come at once to Ottawa in order to present all information direct to you, as to the exact manner in which the proposed treaty will seriously and permanently affect us.
Yours respectfully,
W. C. Bag, Envelope and Box Board Co., Ltd.
(Sgd.) GREELY KOLTS, President.
Now, again, I say I do not wish to reiterate. But isrnot this an awful thing? We in British Columbia have been offering all kinds of inducements to capitalists to establish industries to. work up the millions upon millions of tons of pulpwood that we have in our province. I was myself a member of a Royal Commission to inquire into the handling and conservation of our whole timber resources, and I could occupy this House for hours on that subject alone. We have done everything possible to induce capitalists to establish these industries. We have not only these great supplies of raw material, but we have, as hon. members know, the finest water-poweTS in Canada, and also the coal, and we are there at tidewater. Yet, in the face of these advantages,
*

it has been impossible to get men to go in and start these mills. And to-day we are just beginning. The difficulties of the situation have been set forth here to the Minister of Finance. In the United States the mills have a population of five millions of people immediately surrounding the mills, and forming their home market, while in the province of British Columbia, there is a population of only 300,000. And these people whose letter I have quoted say: If necessary, we will come to Ottawa, not to ask favours, but to explain to the minister. And they get the same answer- ' Too late.' I say it is an awful thing! Why did not the government consult the people of this country? Let me bring this case home to people here-and I am not going to labour the argument. Here we areTn the city of Ottawa. Suppose _any newspaper to-morrow were to suggest the taking awav of the pulp paper industries of Hull, the Eddy and the Booth mills, wiping out the opportunities of employment for the people, but leaving the farmers and owners of pulpwood free to send their wood direct to the United States. Now, I ask: Is there a man, woman or child in Ottawa who would vote in support of that proposition. Yet, that is exactly the position in which we stand in British Columbia. We have all the conditions there for the inception of a successful industry, and we have the capital ready to embark on the enterprise. And yet the minister is prepared by this pact to wipe out the factories we see in imagination and even the one already started, "a photograph of which I have shown. I say again, is not that an awful thing? I am amazed that we should hear from the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller), and even from a minister of the Crown, references to the difference between the automobile owner and the labourer. I say that we are all labourers in Canada, and the man who does something to build up the industries of Canada is deserving of the respect of every man-and I venture to say he receives respect from the vast majority of our people. Every true labourer is working for the good of this great Dominion of ours. I say all honour to the men who, starting with onlv their brains and their hands, have succeeded in building up industries here in Canada. If they have got wealth, I say, God speed and prosper them, for they have helped to build up this Dominion. I would be the last man to destroy these industries. I hope that there is no man in Canada whose vision is so limited, whose sight is so obscured that he would vry by any such argument to sow the seeds of dissension amongst our people. Now, I do not know whether I should go on with these matters-
