WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
I would like to deal with several other subjects in the same practical everyday way. I have briefly touched the main points on the lumber and pulp question. I could cover ' Hansard ' with the representations of these industries of our province, but I will pass on to deal with other matters that interest every man in Canada. The other day I read a paragraph in a newspaper giving facts which struck me, as having a vital bearing on this question. They were all the more important because they were given by one who had no thought of the particular question that is now before us. This item told of Mr. W. S. Workman, of the City Line, speaking at Glasgow on cheap sea-carriage, and the probable effect of oil fuel. Evidently, this gentleman is the manager of one of the large steamship lines in Glasgow, and he was dealing with the outlook of ocean transportation, pointing out that when oil fuel comes into use in vessels, the carrying capacity of the vessels will be materially increased. He gave the number of vessels on the stocks in the different shipbuilding yards of the old country that were to be equipped with the means of using oil as fuel, and went on to show how this would reduce the cost of carriage. This newspaper says that Mr. Workman-
-pointed out that soya beans are brought all the way from Manchuria, a distance of 11,000 miles, for 30s. per ton, while the freight on grain from Glasgow to London is from 10s. to 12s. per ton. Oil, again, is carried from New York to Japan, a distance of 14,000 miles, for about 22s. per ton weight. But the thing comes nearer home when butter, meat, and tea are the subject of examination.
Mr. Workman points out that last year no fewer than 36,000,000 pounds of butter came to us from New Zealand at a freight of only id. per pound, and 3,356,000 carcases of lamb at the same rate per pound. While, too, a pound of tea can be posted to any part of the country for 3d., the shipowner brings it all the way from India for id. per pound, and pays Suez Canal dues into the bargain.
He goes on to argue that when the new vessels are put in commission even these low rates of freight will be reduced. What does that mean? The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Harris) gave the statistics last night, and I do not need to repeat them. All these twelve agricultural countries that are put on the free list by this pact will be in competition with us, not only in the markets of the world, but absolutely in our own markets, right here in Canada. This fact is brought home to us by the information that we get from this absolutely independent and correct source.
Now I want to read a little history of Argentine, and show how that works out. Here is a letter that was handed to me and that illustrates the argument I am making:


Replying to your letter having reference to the importation of chilled meat into Canada under the proposed new reciprocity duty of li cents per pound.	.
We regret very much that we are unahle to give you any figures which would indicate the present price of beef in the Argentine. We hope to be able to do so !n the course of the next few days, when we will write you further.
At the present moment there are 1,500 New Zealand (Canterbury) or Australian lambs on the way to Canada.
1,500 New Zealand lambs on the way to Canada. This is official:
The owners, of course, are figuring on bringing these in paying a 3 cent duty (2 cent preference toVNew Zealand), and selling them in the eastern provinces at just a little better than the price ruling for Canadian lambs. If the duty now 3 cents was reduced to 1} cents it would mean that the Canadian market would have to reduce or decline 1J cents to meet the differential.
Last winter quite a few New Zealand lambs were brought in by the Pacific Coast, and we are informed were sold as far east as Winnipeg.
The lot we have referred to as now on the way to Canada is coming via London, and will arrive at St. John, so that as far as this country is concerned we will be equally affected in the east and in the west by the reduction of this duty. To-day choice young New Zealand mutton, 35-50 pounds, average, are selling in London for about 6 cents, freight and storage f cents, duty 1J cents, proposed, net cost per pound here 7f cents per pound.
Canadian stock of the same class and description is now bringing in from 9 cents to 9J ce*ts in Montreal.
Yet men will stand up in this House and say that it is absurd to talk about the 'competition of Argentine, New Zealand, Denmark, and all these other agricultural countries. I have shown you the actual facts of the present position. Now I want to give you another fact:
Prom the point of view of the manufacturer of meat food products, two facts in connection with the proposed reciprocity movement are not, we think, sufficiently well known.	.	.
There is in Canada a meat inspection law which requires that all meat to be shipped out of the country or to be shipped from one picvince to another shall have passed a post mortem inspection, and shall have been prepared in a proper and sanitary matter. This law co-operates with similar legislation in the United States, and recognizes the inspection certificate of the United States government when attached to the product. This means that American product can come into Canada, into any province, and be reshipped from that province to any other province.
The United States has a similar law, but they do not recognize the inspection certi-cate of the Canadian government, so that while it might seem to an ordinary observer 158
that the Canadian packer would have at his door, under this proposed reciprocity agreement, a very large market on which he could sell some finished product, yet, on examination, this market is found to be absolutely blocked-as small packers in the United States who do not operate under government are few and far between

That is just like the case when they let us have free .fish and put a duty on the cans; it is something similar. Under their law they have a right to keep them in quarantine for thirty days, and you will see what that means:
-while those who do not operate under government inspection could not handle the products of Canadian. packers, because their government will not recognize the certificate of inspection of the Canadian government, and would not allow products so marked to enter the United States inspected packing houses, nor could it be 'shipped from one state to another.
Here I am minded to ask the question, is that reciprocity? I think jot. It is the old jug-handled policy over again, the same old thing I heard of as a boy:
The other point we wish to mention particularly is the stand taken by the Department of Agriculture in regard to the importation of American hogs. The department considers these hogs are not of a sufficiently healthy type to be allowed to come into Canada except after quarantine of sixty days. This would make the import of American hogs impossible-comparatively small packing houses require at least 1,000 per day-to bring in hogs from the United States at the present time would necessitate 60,000 hogs held up in quarantine and a perpetual investment of say $1,000,000 for live stock, which could not bo used for two months from date of purchase. This would be a hardship no packing house could exist under.
Now just another item in regard to butter. I hold in my hand an original telegram absolutely authentic:
Monday, Chicago, March 6,
Lang Racking Co., Mill St., Montreal, ofler 300 tubs or less, June or Sept, storage, creamery 09 pounds ash tubs, medium colour and salt, our score 90 points, 18 cts., Chicago.
P. H. WEAVER & CO.
That butter could be laid down in-Montreal at 184 cents, American butter: I find that the price of a similar quality of butter in Montreal is 24 to 25 cents, and here is-a bona fide offer in the ordinary course of daily business of 300 tubs at a price that would lay it -down at 18J cents. I ask the Canadian farmer what he >
thinks about that kind of reciprocity. Does he consider that his interests have been protected in this matter? Here is another quotation from the New York 'Commercial,' of February 14, 1911:



The total exports of butter from Canada t,o Great Britain in 1909 were 5,353,770 pounds and to the United States 92,468 pounds. The latest available figures for the United States are contained in the census reports for 1900 when New Tort state alone produced upwards of 70,000,000 pounds and the aggregate production of the entire United States was more than a billion pounds.
All this billion pounds of butter comes into competition with the dairy products of the agricultural people of Canada. And here is what they say:
In the year 1909, we imported from Canada less than 100,000 pounds of butter, Canada imported from this country 473,805 pounds. Now when Canada removes her four cents a pound duty upon this product who can measure the amount of butter that this wider market will create for our own farmers? It will be our butter that will be flooding the Canadian market instead of this country being overwhelmed with the Canadian ar-
The egg statistics are equally illuminating, in 1909 Canada's total exports of eggs amounted to about 552,000 dozen, the amount coming to this country being about 52,201 dozen. In tbe same time her imports of eggs aggregated 1,136,120 dozen, so that it appears the country bought twice as much as she exported. The Canadian duty on eggs amounts to three cents a dozen, and with this duty removed the burden is on tbe political farmer to show wby be would not be benefited by this greater market instead of being injured by competition.
And so I could go on all through these statistics. All these favoured nation countries are highly protective, yet we have given the absolute freedom of out market to these twelve countries. No wonder the Finance Minister hesitated to give that information to us.
I think that if I had gone down and made a bargain of that kind I would have been very loath to tell the people about it. It has been said over and over again that Argentina will have no effect on our trade. We have had so many statistics quoted to us that I will not weary you with statistics, but I want to give one or two concise arguments that are based on these statistics and that I know are absolutely correct. I hold in my hand an intensely interesting article that I read several months ago from the ' Journal of the Royal 'Society of Arts, published in London, and dated December 10. When first I read it I had no idea of this treaty coming on. There is an article written for this society by one Campbell J. Ogilvie. It is a most intensely interesting article and covers the whole history of the growth of the agricultural production of Argentina, beginning at the beginning, it is full of illuminating statistics, it contains documents and maps, and it is absolutely accurate. I find that until 1876 Argentina imported wheat for home consumption.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
Argentina exported wheat and food products to Great Britain in 1908 to the amount of one-quarter of the total food products imported into the United Kingdom. Yet that market is absolutely in competition with this market, as I have shown by the transportation route, by the prices and by l the conditions. Now, let us see what Argentina says. The people there are alive to the situation. This subject is so broad that one could take a single phase of it, occupy this House for several hours, and occupy it well, in placing this argument before it. But here is the summing up. After pointing out that they send 25 per cent of the total food products into the United Kingdom and that the United States sends in 33J per cent, the writer of this article says:
The lesson shown her is one worthy of attention. We see that Argentina supplies England with one-fourth of her imported food, and the United States of America supplies nearly one-third. Therefore, it behooves both England and Argentina to see that America does not so manipulate things that she acquires the control over our meat and food supplies.
If it behooves Argentina and Great Britain to see that America does not acquire control over their meat and food supplies', how much more does it behoove the Dominion of Canada to see that America does not acquire control over that trade? Yet, in that connection, what are the facts? I can prove to you by the documents here that that is the exact position and the effect of this treaty. Let me quote again Sir George Ross in regard to it.
We must not forget that the mere exchange of certain articles may involve a great deal more than appears on the surface. For example, to. abolish the duty on wheat on both sides of the line looks fair, but to accept an ofier of that kind pure and simple would, in my opinion, be a poor bargain for Canada. I believe tbat tbe longer tbe American tariff of 25 cents a bushel on Canadian wheat is maintained the better for us-Canadian wheat has now a distinct place in the British market; if the market of the United States were freely opened it would be impossible to maintain its identity in passing through American elevators, and Canada would be the loser to tbe extent of any reduction in price.
Following up the contention of Sir George Ross, I want to read from an official document the statement of the Hon. Philander C. Knox, who made this bargain with the ministers from Canada. What does he say with regard to that?
In providing for free wheat we also take into account the facilities which the United States possesses for handling a part of tbe surplus of Canadian crop and thus preventing the demoralization of prices which results through the dumping of large quantities upon the European markets, where tbe world's price

is fixed. The free admission of grain from Canada thus meets the present situation,,and provides against future contingencies when the Canadian surplus becomes greater by placing the control in the hands of our own grain-growers.
I especially call your attention to that. Mr. Knox says that
The free admission of grain from Canada provides against future contingencies when the Canadian surplus becomes greater by placing the control in the hands of our own grain growers. They have no cause to fear a demoralizing influx under the conditions which will result from the reciprocity agreement.
He says fairly and unmistakably in that paragraph that the result of this agreement willl be to place control of Canadian grain absolutely in the hands of American elevator companies. To show that that is a fact here is what the * Northwestern Miller' says:
The disposition of Canada's surplus is a question upon the answer to which depends the future, not only of the milling interests of the (American) Northwest, but indeed of the United States. Should this surplus be shipped abroad, it must inevitably mean the destruction of the American export trade, the shifting of the American milling centre, the gradual decline of the American milling interest to a purely domestic basis, and its ultimate retrogression to a comparatively unimportant place in the list of large American industries. . . . The miller who is able to grind this enormous (Canadian) crop will be the miller of the future; and, where he is, there will be the great mills of the world.
I commend that to the grain growers of the Northwest, but I shall prove it by the farmers' delegations themselves' because I want to take their authority. Here is what they say as quoted from the official document :
All we have said in regard to the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur, applies equally to elevators that must be constructed in the near future at Hudson's bay and particularly at Pacific coast terminals. The reasons are even more urgent in respect to the Pacific coast than have been advanced for acquiring those at Fort William and Port Arthur. The reasonable and logical way for the grain produced in Alberta and even in the western portion of Saskatchewan to find its market is via what has been termed the * western route.' The western development that is bound to take place in British Columbia in the next decade, assures us that a very large portion of the farm products of Alberta will find a market in this province.
Yet, this pact would force British Colum bia to give its $14,500,000 worth of agricul tural products not for the wheat of Alberto but for the wheat of Washington, Oregon and other American states. But they sak more than that. Mr. Richardson, speaking 158*
on behalf of the grain growers, page 25, said:
1 noticed a statement in a newspaper some time ago that it might be good policy to adopt the Minnesota law. Gentlemen, I think our trouble is all from Minnesota. All the wrinkles, all the knowledge gained in 35 or 40 years of elevator terminals there has been brought to Canada and used in Canada. We were doing much better before the Minnesota people came in. Do not let us go there to look for help. Surely, we are able to help ourselves.
So say I. But that is not all.
I think that our No. 2 Northern to-day is equal to Minnesota No. 1 Northern. 1 think that if I were to lay these two grades down before a miller in New York State, he would give ours the preference. Now, we want to keep it that way; we do not want to weaken our grades. I have always said that we have the best climate, the best people, we can raise the best wheat, and we have the best waterways, let us keep on doing. We are a great country, and we can a fiord to buy these terminal elevators.
He is asking for terminal elevators, but I say the whole argument bears out what the Hon. Philander C. Knox says, what Sir William Van Horne, in his letter, says, what Sir George Ross says, what Mr. J. J. Hill says and what I do not hesitate to say. Mr. Hill has demonstrated a fact which I always believed, namely, that it is not the tariff that has made the difference in the prices of grairt products in the west; that it is due to local conditions of transportation and matters of that kind, and he has proved that beyond all question, by the fact that there is a greater difference in the price between the various states of the union, than there is between the prices in western Canada and the prices in the western states. The position is that if we remove this tariff as the agreement proposes, then the American millers will get in our No. 1 hard northern wheat, mix it with the softer, inferior grain, skin it down as the technical term is, and it will go out to the Liverpool market as No. 1, but barely passing that grading, and it will take a reduced price. The very argument that the millers present for government owned elevators, will be absolutely out of the control of Canada, and it will reflect back on the Canadian farmer, and instead of getting a higher orice, he will get a lesser price. There is i blue-book issued by the Dominion government giving the case of the Manitob" "armers and when you look at their case, md look at what the government has *iven them, you will see that the western uen have literally asked for bread and bey have been given a stone. I have here i letter received by the leader of the oppo-

sition which is very apropos of the situation, and which reads:
Montreal, March 2, 1511.
E. L. Borden, M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
Bear Mr. Borden,-If the Hon. Mr. Fisher is correctly quoted in the Ottawa 'Citizen' of the first instant, lie made a statement to the effect that I had succeeded in getting a reso-1 inti on passed by the Montreal Hoard of Trade condemning -the pro-position before the House, but that two weeks later the 'loyal and imperial Board of Trade of Montreal rescinded that resolution, realizing that the Canadian millers would not Ire injured; inasmuch as they realized that the same agreement opened up to them for their flour a market of ninety millions of people.'
This sentiment apparently was cheered in the House.
I seconded the resolution brought before the Board of Trade by the council at the annual meeting on February first last, and this resolution has not been rescinded. It has been presented bo Sir Wilfrid Laurier in ics original form.
I am not aware of any Canadian millers realizing that by the proposed agreement a market of ninety millions of people to the scuibh of us would he opened up for their flour products. The fact stands out preeminently that the Americans, as mentioned in my recent letter which appeared in the press, maintain a duty on Canadian flour entering their market of 50 cents a barrel and 121 cents per hundred pounds on by-products, or $2.50 per bon.
Surely the Hon. Mr. Fisher was aware that in the agreement now before the House there is a prohibitory duty on both flour and by-products entering the United States from the Canadian miller.
Also as reported in last night's 'Star,' the Hon. Mr. Fisher mentioned my name, that I had headed an article which appeared in the press lately, 'Preserve the Integrity of the Empire,' and stated that he would rather substitute the words, 'Preserve my Preserve for the Benefit of Mr. Meighen,' that the free trade policy would interfere with the monopoly enjoyed by the millers in the northwest in purchasing wheat from the farmer.
The millers are purchasing their wheat in the open market in competition with the Wheat buyers of tbe world. There is no monopoly. I deny tbe assertion that the company I represent is in any combination with any other milling company or private individuals for purchasing wheat either high, or low, or uniform. We run our own business quite independently.
Therefore, the Hon. Mr. Fisher has made quite a mistake in stating that I am striving to preserve a monopoly in the northwest in purchasing wheat.
If his theories are correct, that the arrangement now before the House will give the farmer _ a higher price for his wheat, thereby raising the value of farm lands enormously and also enhancing the value of timber lands covered with a crop of puly wood, then I will inform the Hon. Mr. Fisher that my holdings of farm lands west of the Great Lakes and of timber lands covered with a crop of pulp wood east of the lakes, even at Mr. GOODEVE.
their present value without any alleged enhanced value on account of reciprocity or the trade agreement with the United States, are ten times larger than my interests in the milling business of which I am president.
Therefore, according to the^ hon. gentleman's theories, I am working decidedly against my own interests in opposing the agreement.
I take my stand, however, against the present agreement from national and imperial and commercial grounds, entirely apart from prospective values of the properties in which I a.m interested.
Is it asking too much of you to have a member on your side read any portion of this letter in the House when you may think it favourable, and make my denial as public as the remarks of the Hon. Mr. Fisher have been made, as I believe it is not customary for a member of the House to use the name of a private individual as mine has been used by the Hon. Mr. Fisher.
Yours faithfully,

I have endeavoured to make a fair argument, taking all my statistics from official sources. I think J have shown that in every particular this compact, if carried out, will work to the detriment of the agricultural classes of the people of Canada both east and west.

I am glad he has made that explanation, for I was sorry for the sake of the profession that it would require so many words from a lawyer to put forward the very meagre ideas that were brought forward before this House. There are very few things in my hon. friend's speech that are really of importance and serious. He says that this agreement, if it goes into force, is going to stagger and break up our relations with the mother country. If that is true it is a very serious matter. He makes another charge against the members of this government, who have made the agreement, that they bound us hand and foot to the American government and sacrificed our autonomy, so that we will have no control whatever in future over the making of our own tariffs. That is another very serious charge. He made another statement that this compact was holding a club over the heads of the different provinces of Canada in respect to the question of pulp wood. That is another charge made by the hon. member, which, if true, is very serious. There is nothing better in cases of this kind than to go right to the very source of the matter and find out what is in this agreement to corroborate. or to carry out, or to sustain the statements made by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve).
On the question of being tied hand and foot and our autonomy being hampered in any way let us read the fourth paragraph of the agreement as set forth apd signed by the Canadian plenipotentiaries. Will any ordinary man, whether in this House or out of it, say that there is anything in that paragraph to back up the statement made not only by the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Goodeve) but by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster)?
The only allusion to that phase of the subject is to be found in section 4:
4. The governments of the two countries having made this agreement from the conviction that, if confirmed by the necessary legislative authorities, it will benefit the people on both sides of the border line, we may rea-Mr. McKENZIE.
sonably hope and expect that the arrangement, if so confirmed, will remain in operation for a considerable period. Only this expectation on the part of both governments would justify the time and labour that have been employed in the maturing of the proposed measures. Nevertheless, it is distinctly understood that we do not attempt to bind for the future the action of the TJnited States Congress or the parliament of Canada, but that each of these authorities shall be absolutely free to make any change of tariff policy or of any other matter covered by the present arrangement that may be deemed expedient. We look for the continuance of the arrangement, not because either party is bound to it, but because of our conviction that the more liberal trade policy thus to be established will be viewed by the people of the United States and Canada as one which will strengthen the friendly relations now happily prevailing and promote the commercial interests of both countries.
I ask you what there is in that section to support the very serious charge made against this government by that hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Goodeve). Let us see how that compact is understood by the United States government. Mr. Knox, Secretary of State for the United States, tells us in his letter, and that letter shows that they understand the pact exactly as it is expressed. He says:
Department of State, Washington,
January 21, 1911. The Hon. W. S. Fielding, and The Hon. William Paterson,
Washington.
Gentlemen,-I have the honour to ack-knowledge the receipt of your communication of this Mate in relation to the negotiations initiated by the President several months ago for a reciprocal trade arrangement between the United States and Canada, in which you set forth and ask me to confirm your understanding of the results of our recent conferences in continuation of these negotiations.
I take great pleasure in replying that your statement of the proposed arrangement is entirely in accord with my understanding of it.
There it is set forth clearly and distinctly by our plenipotentiaries that no such binding, no such tying up can possibly be the result of this agreement. The plenipotentiaries of the United States, speaking on their own behalf and on behalf of the President of the United States says he understands the agreement precisely as it is expressed by our plenipotentiaries. There can therefore, be no such binding or trammelling of our rights or interference with our autonomy. I submit, therefore, that the charge made on that point is without foundation so far as the agreement is concerned, and we have nothing else to draw upon but that agreement as submitted to us. A very serious charge was made by the last speaker (Mr. Goodeve), namely, that we were interfering seriously with the autonomy of the provinces and were putting a club in the

hands of the people of the United States by which they might force our provinces into sending pulp wood free of duty into that country. I submit that that charge is just as unfounded as the other. Paragraph 10 of the agreement deals with that point. It is well the people should know exactly what the agreement is and what foundation there is for such serious charges as are made by gentlemen who are opposed to this arrangement
10. With respect to the discussions that have taken place concerning the duties upon the several grades of pulp, printing paper, &c.- mechanically ground wood pulp, chemical wood pulp, bleached and unbleached, news printing paper and other printing paper and board made from wood pulp, of the value not exceeding four cents per pound at the place of shipment-we note that you desire to provide that such articles from Canada shall be made free of duty in the United States only upon certain conditions respecting the shipment of pulp wood from Canada. It is necessary that we should point out that this is a matter in which we are not in a position to make any agreement. The restrictions at present existing in Canada are of a provincial character. They have been adopted by several of the provinces with regard to what are believed to be provincial interests. We have neither the right nor the desire to interfere with the provincial authorities in the free exercise of their constitutional powers in the administration of their public lands. The provisions you are proposing to make respecting the conditions upon which these classes of pulp and paper may be imported into the United States free of duty must necessarily be for the present inoperative. Whether the provincial governments will desire to in any way modify their regulations with a view to securing the free admission of pulp and paper from their provinces into the market of the United States, must bo a question for the provincial authorities to decide. In the meantime, the present duties on pulp and paper imported from the United States into Canada will remain. Whenever pulp and paper of the classes mentioned are admitted into the United States free of duty from all parts of Canada, then similar articles, when imported from the United States, shall be admitted into Canada free of duty. I
I submit that nothing could be plainer or stronger than the statement there made by the Canadian plenipotentiaries. And that statement is that there is no desire to interfere in the slightest degree with the full powers of the provincial authorities to deal with this question. If the provinces, which now have those regulations, wish to continue them, there is nothing to prevent their doing so. And if any other province sees fit to make such regulations, there is nothing in this compact to interfere with that right in the slightest degree. I submit, therefore, that there is not the slightest ground for these two grave charges made by the hon. members opposite in con- nection with this agreement.
A further charge made is that this agreement is going to strike at the loyalty of the Canadian people, that it will switch them off from their attachment to the mother country, and make them Americans. Well, the quotation I am about to make from the report of the British ambassador to Washington will no doubt be accepted by the people of this country, and his opinion is very much stronger than anything I could say. What does Mr. Bryce say on this point. I suppose it would be quite unnecessary to give any certificate of character to this witness, as to the force of his observations or his credibility. But, in case there might be, I will read what was said about him in this House a couple of days ago by no less a personage than the' hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden, Halifax). That hon. gentleman said:
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries ha9 stated that some people in this country had apprehensions as to what might be the result when Mr. Bryce was named the British ambassador at Washington. So far as I am concerned, I have heard of none of these apprehensions and know of no one who entertained them, unless it be the Minister of Marine and Fisheries himself. I believe that Mr. Bryce has acted conscientiously and with ability and energy on behalf of the interests of the mother country and of Canada throughout the course of these difficulties at Washington.
That is the man whose evidence I wish to put before the House in connection with the charge of disloyalty to the interests of the Canadian people as alleged in connection with the negotiations of the agreement which is now undeir consideration in this House. This is the despatch:
London, March 8.-Ambassador Bryce's reports to the foreign office on the subject of the United States-Canada reciprocity negotiations were issued in a white paper this evening. The most interesting communication is under date of January 22, the day following the conclusion of the agreement. In this the British diplomat says:
This is the part I particularly wish to bring forward in answer to my hon. friend from Kootenay:
As at present advised, I am disposed to believe that British interests are not to any appreciable extent prejudiced. No opportunity was lost in the course of the negotiations of reminding the Canadian ministers of the regard which it was right and fitting that they should have to the imperial interests. The arrangement still rests in reality on a growing realization of the fact that a high tariff wall between contiguous countries whose products are economically interchangeable is an injury to both and opposed to sound fiscal principles. In so far as the arrangement oversteps this basis it is probably influenced and will at any rate be publicly justified and defended in the United States, by the traditional policy of the United States of pro-

moting close economic relations with the states of the western hemisphere.
That such a policy is not counteracted by and does not check the rapidly growing sense of national consciousness and international importance in the peoples of those states has of late been abundantly proved.
No more in Canada than in the republics of Latin America to which the United States government has sought to extend its panAmerican propaganda, does there seem a likelihood that a freer interchange of commodities will lead to closer relations of a political kind.
That is the opinion expressed by the right hon. gentleman who occupies the very high and honourable position of Ambassador from His Majesty's government in Great Britain to the United States government at Washington. He is responsible for advising his government and his King as to effect this agreement is likely to have upon the attachment of this nation to the Crown. If it has any tendency to break up our loyal connection with the Crown of England, it would be the duty of this man, his special duty, to so report. He .reports to the very contrary. Therefore, I think the people of Canada, and the people of the British Empire generally, will accept the opinion of so notable a representative of the British nation as Mr. Bryce in preference to any opinion that may be expressed by gentlemen in this House who cannot be expected to have such a wide knowledge of the subject in hand as did the gentleman whose business in particular it was to hold close supervision over this question.
I do not propose to follow any further the observations of my hon. friend from Kootenay. As to whether the interchange of products between this country and the United States is a good thing or a bad thing, I am not in a position to say with any authority. I do not profess to be an exnert in questions of trade. But, as an ordinary individual having ordinary knowledge of the commonplace things that govern trade. I should suppose that this arrangement ought to be a good thing. I believe it is a good thing; and for that reason I intend to support the motion before the House. A great deal has been said, and I suppose a great deal more will be said hereafter, to show that the men we sent to Washington were not fully equipped for the very important business thev had in hand. All I have to say is that, if we are to enteT up6n any agreement at all with a foreign country to extend our trade and better our conditions, in this case we did the very best we could In the party to which I belong, I cannot put my hand upon a better enuipped set of men than those we sent to Washington. The Minister of Finance "(Mr. Fielding), has been for thp last thirty years in train-Mr. McKENZIE.	i
ing in this line of work. For the last fourteen years he has held the position of Minister of Finance of the Dominion and for fourteen years before that he was Prime Minister of Nova Scotia, having charge of its finances. Since he took charge of the finances of the Dominion, he has on two occasions carried on inquiry all over the country on fiscal questions including every subject that possibly could come under consideration at Washington. He was assisted by the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson), a man of almost the same length of training and of immense experience. And these gentlemen had two experts at their elbows. I submit that the Dominion of Canada was as well represented as we could hope it to be-we had no better men. I feel about sending the Minister of Finance to Washington much as the English people felt when they sent their best man to command in the Boer war. They had sent one general after another into the field, and at last they brought forward the veteran, Lord Roberts. We felt that we were in the last ditch, that we had strained every nerve, and that if Lord Roberts could not do the trick we had no one else to send. That, I believe, is the wav the people of Canada felt about the negotiations at Washington-if the Minister of Finance could not succeed, we had nobody else to send who would better the situation. I am satisfied that the Canadian people, at all events the friends of the government and those who can approach this question without bias, will be satisfied that the very best thing had been done for the Dominion of Canada and that the future operations of this agreement will show that the best agreement of a commercial kind for the Dominion of Canada has been made that ever was entered into between this country and any foreign nation, and that another wreath will be placed upon the head of the Minister of Finance as the man who has ably looked after the affairs of this country and in whom the people of this country have good reason to place implicit confidence.
Now, Sir, I cannot understand why it should be a bad thing for us to make a trade agreement with the United States. It will not be said by any person that we should not trade wherever wre can do so-profitably. It will not be said by any person that when we have seven or eight million people alongside a nation with 90 million we should not trade with them, particularly when it is taken into consideration that we have just as great and just as productive a territory as they have, that our object is to grow and become just as large as they are. It must be admitted that our ambition is to grow, and expand in

every direction. I would like to ask those hon. gentlemen who oppose this agreement and ask us to let well enough alone, how they propose to reach that high state of nationhood which all patriotic Canadians have in view. Therefore, if it is right and proper that we should seek expansion of trade, where can we more reasonably hope to obtain it than with our neighbours alongside of us? I think it will be admitted that the 90 or 100 millions of people in the United States, are good customers. They are men largely of our own blood, speaking our own language, having our own high ideals, and they are prepared to use anything that we can supply to them. I think it is admitted that there is abundance of room in the American market for anything we have to sell. We are a new country, and we are not exporting largely the finer class of manufactured goods, but we are exporting largely the products of the sea, of the farm and of the forest. I think it will be admitted that there is abundant room in the United States for the sale of all these articles. If that be true, and if the American people are. willing to buy and to pay the price we ask, can there be any serious objection to trading with them? I submit there is none.
Now, Sir, another objection that is put forward by the opponents of this agreement is, that it will undermine the loyalty of the Canadian people to the British flag. It would seem that if we can assure our Conservative friends that there is no danger in that direction, they would be quite willing to allow this agreement to go into force. We are already dealing with the United States in exports to the extent of something like $114,000,000 per year. For many years we have been doing a profitable trade with the United States, and as a consequence, I do not think there is the slightest trace of disloyalty in the Canadian people. We are also importing into this country something like $250,000,000 worth of goods, and I submit there is not the slightest trace of disloyalty in the Canadian people in consequence of that trade. Now if we can do this enormous trade that we have done in the past without any harm to our loyalty, is it reasonable to suppose that a still larger trade with our United States neighbours will have any such effect? Who can really argue, that a much large trade with them than we have been doing, will have any effect upon our loyalty to the Crown to which we owe allegiance? I say it is a sad reflection on the Canadian people that any person should talk in that way. Where are our Conservative friends going, to find those disloyal people of whom they talk so much? Are they going to find them in British Columbia? I guess not. The people of British Columbia pride themselves on their English origin and their English ideas. Are they going to find these disloyal people in the province of Alberta? There are no such men in that province. Are they going to find them in Saskatchewan or Manitoba? Certainly not. Are they going to find them in the great and loyal province of Ontario? No one supposes for a moment that there are any in that province. Are they going to find them in Quebec? We never heard of any. The people of Quebec have stood their baptism of fire and showed their loyalty to the British Crown more than once. It is not likely that the sale of an ox, or a cow, or a barrel of potatoes, or a ton of hay, by the people of Quebec to the United States, is going to vary that loyalty which has stood the test for 150 years, and no more strenuous circumstances are likely to arise again. In New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, I am sure the people have ptoven their loyalty and their love for the old flag for nearly 200 years, and they are not going to change now.
Now if these things be so, and we can find no trace, no seed of disloyalty in this Dominion, where is the danger of having the fullest and amplest trade with our neighbours? Is there any danger in giving a man who has wheat to sell an opportunity to sell it in England, to sell it in Canada, or to sell it in the .

United States? Have not our people a right to trade to any extent with any of these countries? Have not the men who raise wheat in the Northwest a right to sell it in Winnipeg, or in Montreal, or across the border, wherever they could get the best price? No one will make the assertion that the Canadian farmer is incapable of competing with the American farmer, or any other man on earth, in the production of grain. He has the capacity to bargain for the sale of it, he has the capacity to arrange for its transportation. If that be the case, if we have the transportation facilities, and if we have the products, why should we not seek a market for them? If the English market is open to us to-day, and if it is the best, surely we have common sense enough to hold it. If we can get more money for our wheat in the Canadian market, surely we can trust the Canadian farmer to sell it in Montreal, Winnipeg or Toronto. If he finds that he can sell his wheat in the United States to better advantage than in the Canadian market, whose business is it to interfere with him? Is it not the duty of this government to place the widest possible market at his disposal? That has been the theory of the Conservative party as well as of the Liberal party for the last forty years, at all events, ever since confederation. There has

been no party in power or in opposition in Canada that has not been favourable to better trade relations with the United States than we could usually have.
There is a great cry that we have no mandate to make this agreement. If this is a good bargain, if it is a good proposition for the Canadian people, if it is a good thing for the farmer, for the lumberman, for the men who have manufactured goods to sell, if it gives the manufactured article any advantage, is the manufacturer or the farmer going to say to the Canadian plenipotentiaries : True, I can sell my wheat, my horses, my sheep, or my goods better, but I do not think I will take advantage of this agreement because you had no mandate from the people when you made it. That would be carrying the matter to an extreme absurdity, and I am reminded of a story of the man who was so extremely strong on the eight-hour law that he allowed himself to drown after he had been eight hours in the water rather than transgress it. He said that he would not break the eight-hour law, but that he would rather die in the water than try to save himself he had struggled for eight hours. That is a very extreme case, but it would appear to me that the farmer, or mechanic, or lumberman who wished to find fault with this agreement by saying that there was no mandate would be in the same class as the extraordinary man who would not save his life, after he had struggled in vain for eight hours.	.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I wish to pay a little further attention to some observations that were made about the prosperous condition of this country, and before I reach that I wish to say something about the province of Nova Scotia, and the coal question. I suppose the coal industry is the largest of any one industry in Canada. The coal industry of Nova Scotia has a capital invested in it of something in the vicinity of $100,000,000, it has 10,000 or 12,000, possibly more, men directly dependent upon it, and for us in Nova Scotia the coal question is a very important one indeed. At the same time, we realize that we are part and parcel of the country, that it takes all kinds of people to make a world, and that all manner of agreements, give and take must be made in order that we shall get along peaceably and harmoniously the one with the other. That being the case, and knowing that there must be revenues raised in this country and that the consumer must also be taken into consideration, the consideration of this question all manner of agreements, give and take, must be made. Speaking as one representing the coal industry of Nova Scotia, while we would like to have seen the duty remain as it was, and while we think it would have been perfectly Mr. McKenzie.
justifiable to let it remain, we are content to take our share of the burden of taxation upon the people, and if eight cents a ton has been taken off that coal we must put up with it, and do the best we can. I think that with the fair start the coal industries have made, with the standing they have attained nQw, and the character of the article that we are producing, we will be able to stand the strain that may be cast upon us by reason of this reduction. However, I notice in a paper published in Sydney that it is cast up to the premier of Nova Scotia, and my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that they have never done anything for the coal trade, and that they have always been trying to hurt it. I want to state that in so far as I can learn there is nothing on record in the history of the Conservative party that would indicate or in any way satisfactorily prove that they have ever done anything for the coal industries of Nova Scotia. The coal industries of Nova Scotia have a history, and that history shows that nothing was done for them worthy to be mentioned by the National Policy. Our friends speak of the National Policy as the only thing that they ever produced that is worthy of praise or mention. What is this National Policy? A stranger coming into this country would think that it was some great, herculean act performed by the Conservative party of that day that had brought about the greatest possible amount of prosperity and expansion in this country. What does it amount to? Before the adoption of the National Policy in 1879 we had a tariff of 17i per cent, and the Conservative party raised that to something around 25 per cent. That is all that the National Policy is, nothing else; no great statesmanship about it, no great difficulty about raising a tariff from 17J to 25 per cent, or a little higher, or as high as you like. There is nothing wonderful about it. That is all the National Policy is, and what has it done for the coal industry of Nova Scotia? I am talking here in the presence of members of this House, what I say will go before the coal owners of Nova Scotia and the people I represent. Talking, therefore, in this place and subject to criticism, I submit, Sir, that while the coal industries of Nova Scotia had nothing to go- upon but the National Policy it was simply dragging along, and starving. You will find the Halifax 'Herald ' of September, 1906, reporting that in those days of the National Policy coal was simply capable of giving half time and half pay to its people, and that it was on the ragged edge of poverty. That is the way that paper speaks in an article written by Mr. Milner who professes to be an authority on the coal question. From 1878 to 1893 we had nothing in Nova Scotia, but the National Policy in

so far as the coal industry is concerned. During the whole of that period the highest year's output in the Island of Cape Breton was only 700,000 tons-a very small output and produced by half time and half pay, according to the Halifax ' Herald.' In those days the hon. gentleman who is now the Finance Minister was the Prime Minister of Nova Scotia. He came to the conclusion that something had to be done, and that an improvement ought -to be made in the conditions of affairs in Nova Scotia. He set about bringing American capital into Nova Scotia for the purpose of improving the conditions of the coal trade.
What happened in these days is just what is happening in this House to-day. He was met with the most strenuous opposition from the Conservatives in the local legislature; he was told that what he was doing would reduce the thousands of miners of Nova Scotia to the position of serfs, depriving them of their manhood and liberty; that they would be subject to the combines and riionopolies of the United States; that the Americans were purchasing the Cape Breton mines to close them down and that ruin would follow. Any one who reads the speeches of the then leader of the opposition in the local House, Mr. Cahan, will realize that I am not overdrawing the picture. In the face of all that, the Hon. Mr. Fielding, then Prime Minister of Nova Scotia, went on with the agreement, and as a result $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 of capital was invested in this industry, and where we were then exporting 700,000 tons of coal per annum we are to-day exporting over 5,000,000 tons, and the towns and hamlets which had then a population of two and three thousand are to-day cities of twenty thousand people. Where we then had many disjointed companies with small mines we have to-day this magnificent development of the Dominion Coal Company, and the Dominion Steel Company, and the Tar and Chemical Company, and the cement companies and others, none of which would be in existence were it not for the policy laid down by the Hon. Mr. Fielding, who was then in charge of the destinies of Nova Scotia. At that time, Senator MacKeen, who was then a member of this parliament, and whose Conservatism will not be questioned, because he vacated his seat in this House to make room for Sir Charles Tupper when it was found necessary to bring him back into politics to try and redeem the fortunes of the Conservative party; Senator MacKeen, because of the character of the Tory opposition to this great scheme, found it necessary to write, in the interests of Nova Scotia and of Canada, as follows: I
I believe that legislation by which alone it was possible to bring capital in/bo the country for the development of our coal and iron industries to an extent far beyond the capacity of Great Breton capitalists to invest, is, and must be, for the good of the whole province, and should not be condemned but encouraged by every one having an interest in the prosperity and welfare of our country.
I have no sympathy with parties who, prompted by political passions, deliberately denounce measures which, if successfully carried out, must result in public good; and such a course seems to me to say very little for the intelligence of those persons who pursue it.
They still hold them and with the exception of two small mines which could not be worked to a profit, they are working more vigorously than ever. A company which only purchases indues in order to close them does not commence to build forty miles of rail-read at a cost of upwards of half a million dollars and push the w'ork forward with the utmost despatch. Nor does it entirely rebuild a large shipping pier at a further outlay of nearly $300,000, and this is what the Dominion Coal Company are doing with the railroad from Bridgeport to Lonishurg, and with the old international pier. Surely this alone would by all reasonable men be accepted as a sufficient contradiction to this mean slander.	_
Depend upon it, this company has come to stay, and the above facts should effectually silence those cavillers who for purposes of their own have tried to arouse the fears and stimulate the hostility of the miners of Cape Breton by falsely alleging that the policy of the company would deprive them of employment in the future.
I think those who seek for any reason to stir up opposition to a company which has introduced such an enormous amount of capital into the island, and which is laying itself out to provide employment for a far greater number of miners than are at present employed in the industry, is no friend to the inhabitants of Cape Breton, and fails altogether _ to appreciate the important consequences which I firmly believe will follow the establishment of this concern.
That was the language Senator MacKeen used under conditions which to my mind were very similar to the conditions which exist to-day. We were then in Nova Scotia bringing about a new condition of things, we were getting more capital into the country, and the Conservatives told us as they are telling us to-day: leave well enough alone, what we have we hold, don't do anything for the advancement of this country but just stand where you are. Well, the Liberals went on with their policy in Nova Scotia and development and progress followed, and it was due not to the National Policy but to what is known as the Whitney legislation and the enterprise and foresight of the Minister of Finance, who tonight leads this House. Our Conservative friends have criticised the representatives from Nova Scotia in this House because we are willing to agree to a cut of eight cents a ton on the duty on coal and-they tell us what marvellous things they would do for

us if they had control. There is no better means of arriving at what people would do if they had the power than to take what they say when they are out of power, and, when a few evenings ago the leader of the government spoke upon this very important question, the member for North Simcoe (Mr. Ourrie) was put up as the representative of the opposition to reply to the First Minister. We have a right to assume that the leader of the opposition did not put up the hon. member for North Simcoe without some consideration to answer the most important speech that will be made on this great question, and which was delivered by the Prime Minister, who was listened to with greater interest on this question than would be any other man in the country. I suppose the leader of the opposition did not mean any discourtesy to the Prime Minister when he put forward the hon. member for North Simcoe, on the contrary I would expect that the hon. gentleman submitted to the leader of the opposition what he was going to say, . and that anything he did say on so grave an occasion had the full sanction of his leader. On the question of protection foT coal this is what was said by the hon. member for North Simcoe, who represented the leader of the opposition on that important occasion:
If Nova Scotia continues to send such men to this House, and there is no doubt from the signs of the times that there will be a change in the next parliament, I for one, staunch protectionist as I am, will have to consider whether it is worth while for the rest of the country to grant a duty of 50 cents a ton to Nova Scotia on coal and a bounty on her steel.
That is the threat which is held over our heads by the gentleman who spoke for the opposition in answer to the speech of the Prime Minister. Later on, I think it was yesterday, another front bencher of very high standing I suppose in the Conservative party, evidently very close to the leader of the opposition, and, I presume, when talking on trade questions, voicing the ideas of that hon. gentleman; I refer to the hon. member for Hastings (Mr, Northrup), spoke on the question of protection to coal, and said:	,
We only bear the duty on coal and iron in consideration of a ditty on our products, and since that was the direct bargain made in 1878 and renewed since, as you have broken the bargain, and removed our duties, we will insist that the duty on coal and iron he removed in order that justice may he done.
That is what we have to expect if our friends on the other side should come into power, and .1 submit, Sir, that on the question of coal, as I have already explained, whatever is done to-day in the province of Nova Scotia, whatever strides the industry has made, have been made, not because Mr. McKENZIE
of any assistance or support received from the national policy, as I have pointed out that during the ten years of the national policy the great property now known as the Dominion Coal Company coal areas, and that of the Nova Scotia Steel Company across the water, together only produced 700,000 tons of coal, whereas to-day the same properties are producing, under the new legislation, something over 5,000,000 tons, all brought about by what is known as the Whitney legislation, a new departure from the old road, in which we travelled for 20 years before that departure was made. I submit that the occasion was much like the present, and that we in Nova Scotia followed the Premier in those days and followed him to success in the teeth of the most vigorous opposition the Conservatives could make to the project. I submit we have a perfect right, and we are bound, I think, to place every confidence in the scheme that the Finance Minister has set before us to-day, believing that the same results will follow.

speechtext: When was the duty put on soft coal?

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS-INFORMATION RE RECIPROCITY AGREEMENT.
speechtext:
A duty was put on soft coal as far back as 1870 or 1871. It was taken off by our Conservative friends when they were in power before 1878, and in 1878 it went on again, but my submission is not that the Conservatives put the duty on or took it off; I am arguing, and I think successfully, that the duty was not sufficient and did not give any impetus to the coal industry in Nova Scotia, and the standing of the coal industries in Nova Scotia to-day is not due to the national policy, but to the Whitney legislation introduced and carried forward by the Hon. Mr. Fielding, then Prime Minister of the province of Nova Scotia. I said, further, that the cry then was to be satisfied with what we had and go no further.
There is one thing more that I propose to say in connection with this matter while we are answering the charges made against us by the Sydney ' Post ' on thfs coal question. They say that the Minister of Finance and the Premier of Nova Scotia were always the enemies and never the friends, and that the duty was, of course, the saviour of that coal question, and that were it not for the duty the death knell of the coal industry in Nova Scotia would have been struck long ago. What did Sir John Macdonald say about the coal duty when we in Nova Scotia were told by the Conservatives that we could not get along without the coal duties, but that every miner would be thrown out of employment, that the pit mouths would be closed if the duty was taken off? On the 30th day of July. 1890, in the midst of this condition, and when our Conservative friends were holding forth that the only

friends of this industry were Sir John Macdonald and his government, he writes this letter to an American gentleman of high standing in the cabinet of that day:
My Dear Sir,-In answer to your esteemed note of this day, I desire to say that I am fully assured that the parliament of Canada will he ready to take off all duties on coal, ores and lumber imported from the United States whenever Congress makes these articles free of duty. The Canadian government has already ,aufchorized_ Sir Julian Pauncefote to state to the American government that they will be prepared to take off the export duty on logs whenever Canadian lumber is admitted into the United States at the reduced rate of one dollar per thousand board measure. You are at liberty to show this to the members of Congress and the President as you please. It should not, for obvious reasons, be published in the press or quoted in Congress. In the United States Tariff Act prevision might be made for making the above-mentioned articles free whenever they are made free by the Canadian parliament.
I remain, my dear sir, faithfully yours, (Sgd.) JOHN A. MACDONALD.
